Assessment: subjective data (HPI, ROS, PMH), objective data (physical exam), ordering, performing and interpreting diagnostic and screening tests.
Diagnosis: formulate and prioritize differentials, recognize urgent and emergent conditions, establish a confirmatory diagnosis.
Planning: patient-centered plan, immediate referrals and consultations, pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapy, education, counseling and health promotion.
Evaluation: effectiveness of the plan, barriers to care, modifying the plan, additional referral, monitoring ongoing response.

Stewardship prevents overuse, misuse and abuse, minimizes resistance, reduces cost. The 5 Ds: Drug (right drug, right bug), Dosing (optimal), Drug route, Duration (suitable), De-escalation (timely to pathogen-directed therapy). Susceptibility does not equal…

Duration: most indications 5–7 days; expect clinical improvement at 48 hours. Longer: strep pharyngitis 10 days, pyelonephritis 14 days, severe infections, immunocompromised patients, many pediatric indications.
Empiric therapy = first-line drug targeting the most likely organisms. Weigh risk of morbidity/mortality (higher risk → broader spectrum), side-effect risk, contraindications, the local antibiogram.
ESKAPE resistant pathogens: Enterococci, S. aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter.

Culture when: patient cannot afford treatment failure; severe infection; risk of complications; unsure of organism or whether infection is present; failed empiric treatment; high resistance risk (recent antibiotics). The site/sample must be appropriate.

Penicillins and cephalosporins share the beta-lactam ring. It matters for allergy (cross-reactivity) and for resistance (beta-lactamase destroys the ring). IgE cross-reactivity is very uncommon; it is most likely when the R1 side chain is similar: 1–8% with…

Rule 1 — NEVER give a 1st-generation cephalosporin if the PCN reaction was anaphylaxis or hives. IgE-mediated type I reactions worsen with each exposure. Other IgE signs: hypotension, laryngeal edema, wheezing, angioedema, urticaria.
Rule 2 — Cautious use of 2nd/3rd-generation cephalosporins after a type I reaction. Dissimilar side chains mean less cross-reactivity; less still if >10 years since the reaction.
Rule 3 — Any cephalosporin may be given if the PCN reaction was a morbilliform rash (maculopapular drug eruption, T-cell mediated, type IV).
Look · Hives: Raised wheals; red on light skin, hypopigmented on dark skin; lesions change size/shape · Morbilliform rash: Maculopapular, coalescing, extremities and trunk; spares mucous membranes
Itch · Hives: Intense · Morbilliform rash: Mild itch/burn
Course · Hives: Sudden, spreads quickly, escalates each exposure · Morbilliform rash: Common in children
Causes · Hives: — · Morbilliform rash: Beta-lactams, quinolones, sulfas, infection, NSAIDs, antiepileptics
Mechanism · Hives: Type I (IgE) · Morbilliform rash: Type IV (T cell)
Beating beta-lactamase: penicillin → amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin); cephalosporins → 3rd generation.

Chronic inflammation causes structural change and persistent, progressive airflow obstruction. Airway abnormalities → chronic bronchitis; alveolar abnormalities → emphysema. Symptoms: progressive dyspnea, chronic cough, recurrent respiratory infections.

Risk factors — GET: Genes (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, rare) · Environment (smoking/exposure, vaping, cannabis, air pollution, indoor stoves, animal dung, crop residues, chemicals) · Time / lung-function trajectory (prematurity, low birth weight,…
Differential: Chronic bronchitis · Characteristics: Normal spirometry; productive cough >3 months for 2 consecutive years (may develop COPD)
Differential: Asthma · Characteristics: May coexist; early-life asthma; chronic obstructive asthma
Differential: Heart failure · Characteristics: Dilated heart on CXR; pulmonary/peripheral edema
Differential: Pulmonary embolism · Characteristics: Risk factors; vague symptoms for weeks; tachypnea, rales, pleuritic pain; D-dimer; CXR atelectasis/opacities; CT angiography confirms
Differential: Tuberculosis · Characteristics: Communal living; fever, cough, pleuritic pain; CXR cavitation/infiltrate; microbiologic confirmation
Differential: Bronchiectasis · Characteristics: Large volumes of purulent sputum; CT bronchial wall thickening and dilation
Diagnosis: symptoms + risk factors + spirometry. FEV1 = air forcefully exhaled in 1 s; FVC = total exhaled in one breath. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7.

mMRC: 4 · Breathlessness: Too breathless to leave the house, or breathless dressing

Goals: reduce symptoms (relief, exercise tolerance, health status) AND reduce risk (minimize progression, prevent/treat exacerbations, reduce mortality). Quitting smoking slows progression but does not stop COPD from worsening.

Exacerbation: ↑ dyspnea and/or cough and sputum worsening over <14 days, ± tachypnea, tachycardia. Triggers: viruses (influenza, rhinovirus), bacteria (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. pneumoniae), pollutants, excessive heat. Rule out pneumonia, PE, HF.

Vaccines for COPD and asthma: influenza annually; RSV (pregnant 32–36 weeks, ≥60 at risk, ≥75); pneumococcal; Tdap every 10 years; COVID-19.

Screen generally healthy adults 50–80 with a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within 15 years (USPSTF; ACS: ever smoked). Screening = secondary prevention; test = low-dose CT, annually.

Smoking cessation: motivational interviewing; assess readiness at every visit and tailor to it. Set a quit date ~2 weeks out. Varenicline, bupropion and combination long-/short-acting NRT are equally effective. Behavioral tips: avoid triggers; 5-minute delay…

Anemia is a reduction in at least one RBC measure — RBC count, hemoglobin, or hematocrit — and is never normal. Exam checklist: IDA, thalassemia, anemia of chronic disease, G6PD deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, thrombocytopenia, CBC differential…
"Normal doesn't always mean normal": a perimenopausal patient whose Hgb falls from 14.6 to 12.5 g/dL after a heavy cycle (normal 12.1–15.2) with SOB and fatigue has a real problem.
MCV (size, "-cytic"): <80 fL · Microcytic · MCH (color, "-chromic"): <26 pg · Hypochromic
MCV (size, "-cytic"): 80–96 fL · Normocytic · MCH (color, "-chromic"): 26–33 pg · Normochromic
MCV (size, "-cytic"): >96 fL · Macrocytic · MCH (color, "-chromic"): >33 pg · Hyperchromic
Reticulocytes (immature RBCs): normal 0–2.5% in adults; reflect marrow production. Anemia should raise the count; anemia with a low retic count means the marrow isn't responding.
RDW (variation in RBC size): <15% normal, >15% abnormal.
Iron panel: serum iron = circulating; ferritin = storage; TIBC = capacity to bind/move iron. Egg-carton analogy: high iron → low TIBC; low iron → high TIBC.
Peripheral smear: a visual description of the cells; consider for any anemia.
Common: iron deficiency, thalassemia. Less common: anemia of chronic disease (<20%), sideroblastic anemia, lead toxicity (presents just like IDA).
Iron-deficiency anemia — microcytic, hypochromic. Causes: blood loss (most common, GYN or GI); low intake, poor absorption, pregnancy. Usually asymptomatic until Hgb ≤10.
Age: Young / middle adult · Presentation: Fatigue, weakness, headache, irritability, exercise intolerance
Age: Older adult · Presentation: Exacerbation of comorbidities (angina, HF, dementia)
Iron-rich foods: liver, lentils, spinach, clams/oysters, red beans, rice, fortified grains.
Iron source (325 mg): Ferrous fumarate · Elemental iron: 106 mg (33%)
Iron source (325 mg): Ferrous sulfate · Elemental iron: 65 mg (20%)
Iron source (325 mg): Ferrous gluconate · Elemental iron: 36 mg (11.6%)
Iron source (325 mg): Extended-release (••) · Elemental iron: Varies (~150 mg)
Elemental iron: old recommendation 150–200 mg daily; new recommendation 15–20 mg daily.

Thalassemia — genetic abnormality of hemoglobin formation → abnormal RBCs, hemolysis or impaired erythropoiesis. Microcytic, hypochromic; target cells on smear. Diagnostic test: hemoglobin electrophoresis.
Hgb, Hct · Thalassemia: Low · Iron-deficiency anemia: Low
MCV, MCH · Thalassemia: Low · Iron-deficiency anemia: Low

TIBC · Thalassemia: Normal · Iron-deficiency anemia: High
Ferritin · Thalassemia: Normal · Iron-deficiency anemia: Low

Anemia of chronic disease (chronic inflammation) — RBC lifespan 60–90 days (normal 100–120). Normocytic, normochromic (long-standing may become microcytic, hypochromic). Causes: RA, morbid obesity, colon cancer, uncontrolled DM, CHF, COPD, CKD, autoimmune…

B12 (cobalamin) and folate (B9) together form RBCs, WBCs and platelets and are needed for DNA/RNA; deficiency of either causes megaloblastic anemia. Usually asymptomatic; severe B12 deficiency gives unexplained neurologic symptoms — cognitive changes,…
Mechanism: ↓ intake · B12 deficiency: Alcohol misuse, severely restricted diet, malnourishment · Folate deficiency: Same

Mechanism: Impaired absorption · B12 deficiency: Pernicious anemia, colchicine; GI alterations (gastrectomy, ileitis, diverticulosis, sprue, celiac, Crohn, bariatric surgery, H. pylori) · Folate deficiency: Hereditary folate malabsorption; same GI alterations
Mechanism: Impaired metabolism · B12 deficiency: H2 blockers, metformin, PPIs, GLP-1 agonists · Folate deficiency: Antiseizure drugs, triamterene, TMP-SMX, metformin, methotrexate
Mechanism: ↑ needs · B12 deficiency: Pregnancy, lactation, hemodialysis, cancer, hyperthyroidism · Folate deficiency: Same

Platelets <150,000; petechiae, purpura and bleeding are far more likely below 50,000. A patient presenting only with a petechial rash needs a CBC.
CBC pattern: Rest of CBC normal · Etiology: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP, "idiopathic"); resolved viral/bacterial infection
CBC pattern: + Leukocytosis · Etiology: Infection, inflammation, malignancy
CBC pattern: + Anemia · Etiology: Sepsis, autoimmune, nutrient deficiency (folate, B12), infection, leukemia, drug-induced

Cell: Eosinophils · Normal: 1–4% · Function: Allergy, asthma, drug reactions, parasites
Cell: Basophils · Normal: 0.5–1% · Function: Nonspecific immunity; release histamine and heparin; recognize new pathogens

Conditions · WBC increased by: Autoimmune/inflammatory disease, bacterial and viral infection, allergy, leukemia/Hodgkin, burns or surgery, smoking · WBC decreased by: Autoimmune (RA, lupus), infection (hepatitis, TB, sepsis, Lyme), lymphoma, leukemia,…

Always interpret with clinical correlation. Polys and lymphs similar → think viral. Elevated WBC with polys and lymphs far apart, and bands present → bacterial.

Sensation of spinning, movement or disequilibrium with many etiologies — get a thorough history. Peripheral = vestibular system/inner ear (BPPV, otitis media, Ménière). Central = brainstem or cerebellum (stroke, MS, brain tumor, meningitis).
Workup: full neuro exam; Dix–Hallpike (canalithiasis of the posterior semicircular canal = BPPV); HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew — abnormal suggests central).
Finding: Nystagmus · Peripheral: Stops with visual fixation · Central: Continues with fixation
Finding: Gait/balance · Peripheral: Normal · Central: Impaired
Finding: Hearing · Peripheral: May be impaired · Central: Normal
Finding: Neuro exam · Peripheral: Normal · Central: Impaired
Etiology: BPPV (peripheral) · Duration: Seconds · History: Triggered by position change; N/V · Exam: Positive Dix–Hallpike
Etiology: Vestibular migraine (peripheral) · Duration: Minutes–hours · History: Migraine history, visual aura, photophobia, severe HA · Exam: Abnormal balance during episodes
Etiology: Vestibular neuritis (peripheral) · Duration: Days; single episode · History: Preceding viral syndrome · Exam: Horizontal nystagmus toward healthy ear; resolves with fixation
Etiology: Ménière (peripheral) · Duration: 20 min–12 h · History: Spontaneous; fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus · Exam: Low/mid-frequency hearing loss
Etiology: TIA (central) · Duration: Usually <1 h · History: Vascular RF, older; sudden; single or recurrent · Exam: Temporary deficits; multidirectional nystagmus
Etiology: Stroke (central) · Duration: Days–weeks, persistent · History: Vascular RF; sudden · Exam: Deficits; possible hemodynamic instability; multidirectional nystagmus
Etiology: MS (central) · Duration: Hours–days · History: Fatigue, sensory loss; relapsing-remitting · Exam: Optic neuritis; intermittent neuropsychiatric changes

BPPV is managed in primary care: Epley repositioning; first-generation antihistamine — best evidence meclizine (Antivert) 25–100 mg, reserved for highly disruptive symptoms (watch anticholinergic effects); antinausea meds. Refer for everything except BPPV.

CT head criteria (New Orleans Criteria / Canadian CT Head Rule): Suspected skull fracture · Open, depressed or basilar; hemotympanum, periorbital bruising, otorrhea, rhinorrhea
CT head criteria (New Orleans Criteria / Canadian CT Head Rule): Bleeding risk · Bleeding disorder or anticoagulant; high-velocity injury (MVA, fall >3 ft); age >60 (NOC), ≥65 (CCHR)

Concussion (mild acute TBI): progressive improvement within 7–10 days; resolution by 1 month; may need school/work accommodations. Symptoms: emotional lability/irritability, headache, dizziness, abnormal balance, mental fogginess, concentration/memory…
Graduated return to play: Day 1 · Activity: ADLs; increase in activity
Graduated return to play: Day 2 · Activity: Light aerobic exercise; increase HR
Graduated return to play: Day 3 · Activity: Sport-specific exercise; add movement
Graduated return to play: Day 4 · Activity: Non-contact training drills; exercise, coordination, thinking
Graduated return to play: Day 5 · Activity: Full-contact practice; restore confidence, coach assesses skills
Graduated return to play: Day 6 · Activity: Full activity
If symptoms recur, go back to the previous step for a minimum of 24 hours; don't advance until symptoms resolve.

CN VII palsy: idiopathic, acute, spontaneous facial paralysis; clinical diagnosis. House–Brackmann grades I (normal) to VI (complete paralysis). Findings: forehead flattening, drooping, loss of nasolabial fold, poor eyelid closure, altered tearing (dry or…
Glucocorticoids: All H–B grades; start ≤72 h from onset; 60–80 mg daily × 7 days, then taper · Antivirals: H–B grade IV or higher with evidence of herpes; ≤72 h
Course: peak 1–2 days → stable ~3 weeks → improving 2–3 months → recovery 3–6 months. Prevent complications: corneal abrasion and psychological distress.
Primary (overactivity of pain-sensing structures): migraine, tension, cluster. Secondary (underlying pathology, often red flags): sinusitis, medication overuse, hypertension, stroke.

Secondary headache: CVA or TIA · Key features: CVD history; sudden focal neuro change; hemodynamic instability; abnormal exam
Secondary headache: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) · Key features: Transient vision changes; papilledema
Secondary headache: Subdural hematoma · Key features: Trauma or blood thinners; insidious neural decline; may be unprovoked
Secondary headache: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis · Key features: Age >50; temple pain, fever, fatigue, jaw claudication, vision changes; ↑ESR/CRP
Secondary headache: Trigeminal neuralgia · Key features: Acute, severe, stabbing unilateral facial pain (CN V distribution); may have pain between attacks

Migraine without aura (ICHD-3): 4–72 h; ≥2 of unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe, aggravated by routine activity; ≥1 of N/V, photophobia or phonophobia; ≥5 attacks (<5 = "probable migraine"); no other cause. With aura: ~25% of migraineurs; meets migraine…
Acute migraine treatment: Simple analgesics · Drugs: Acetaminophen · Considerations: Mild–moderate headache
Acute migraine treatment: NSAIDs · Drugs: Aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac · Considerations: Watch CIs/AEs; more effective combined with triptans
Acute migraine treatment: Triptans · Drugs: Suma-, zolmi-, nara-, riza-, almo-, ele-, frovatriptan · Considerations: CI: basilar migraine, ischemic stroke, MI, Prinzmetal angina, uncontrolled HTN
Acute migraine treatment: CGRP antagonists · Drugs: Zavegepant (Zavzpret, intranasal), ubrogepant (Ubrelvy), rimegepant (Nurtec ODT, also prophylactic) · Considerations: Expensive
Acute migraine treatment: 5-HT1F agonist · Drugs: Lasmiditan (Reyvow) · Considerations: Not vasoconstrictive; may reduce N/V; not first-line

Medication overuse headache (ICHD-3): preexisting headache disorder; headache ≥15 days/month; regular overuse >3 months — >10 days/month of ergotamines, triptans, opioids or combination analgesics, or >15 days/month of simple analgesics; no better…

Prophylaxis indications: >4 attacks/month or >12 h per attack; significant disability; risk of MOH; abortives ineffective, contraindicated or poorly tolerated; menstrual migraine. 3–6 month trial; start low, titrate.

Prophylactic class: Nonselective beta-blockers · Drug: Timolol, propranolol, metoprolol* · Considerations: Good with angina, HTN, anxiety, younger patients. AE: weight gain, fatigue, ↓BP/HR, activity intolerance, bronchospasm. Avoid in bradycardia; caution…
Prophylactic class: Anticonvulsants · Drug: Valproate · Considerations: Weight gain, somnolence, hair loss; highly teratogenic
Drug: Topiramate · Considerations: Weight loss, concentration problems, fatigue, anorexia, paresthesia; avoid in pregnancy
Prophylactic class: Antidepressants · Drug: Amitriptyline* · Considerations: Sedating, give in evening; anticholinergic
Drug: Venlafaxine* · Considerations: Good with panic, GAD, SAD, MDD; nausea, dizziness, insomnia

Criteria · Tension-type: ≥10 episodes with ≥2 of: bilateral, pressing (non-pulsating), mild–moderate, not aggravated by activity; plus ≤1 of photophobia/phonophobia and no N/V · Cluster: ≥5 attacks of severe unilateral orbital/temporal pain with ≥1…

Acute · Tension-type: NSAIDs, aspirin, acetaminophen, acetaminophen-aspirin-caffeine; no opioids or barbiturates · Cluster: 100% oxygen; SQ or nasal sumatriptan
Diabetic neuropathy = distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN). 15–20% have pain. Symptomatic neuropathy is not usually reversible — prevention.

Category: Diffuse motor without sensory · Examples: Guillain–Barré, myasthenia gravis
Category: Inflammatory/infectious · Examples: Sarcoidosis, lupus, Lyme

Diabetic neuropathy drugs (likely on exam): TCAs · FDA-approved: — · Evidence-based off-label: Amitriptyline, desipramine, nortriptyline

All tremors are essential tremor until proven otherwise
Valproic acid treats essential tremor; propranolol treats drug-induced tremor

Unilateral resting foot tremor: Parkinson. Symmetric voice and head tremor: essential. Valproic acid: drug-induced. Primidone or propranolol: essential. With bradykinesia and rigidity: Parkinson. With anxiety and heat intolerance: hyperthyroidism.

patient is always aware of impairment
determine whether the family member has medical POA.

Covers depression, bipolar screening, suicidality, anxiety, PTSD, substance use, adult ADHD and insomnia. Know presentation, screenings, criteria, differentials, management, course, follow-up and when to refer.

Mood is shaped by biology (neurotransmitters, hormones), psychology, physiologic state and environment. Stimuli: fatigue, hunger, stress, fear, anger, genetics, toxins; the postsynaptic impulse is excitatory or inhibitory.
Neurotransmitter: Serotonin (5-HT) · Impulse: Inhibitory · Role: Appetite, mood, anxiety, sleep, sex drive
Neurotransmitter: Dopamine · Impulse: Excitatory and inhibitory · Role: Energy, reward, motivation, mood, attention, executive function
Neurotransmitter: GABA · Impulse: Inhibitory · Role: Calm and relaxation; anxiety and sleep
Neurotransmitter: Norepinephrine · Impulse: Excitatory · Role: Mood, alertness, concentration, energy
Neurotransmitter: Epinephrine · Impulse: Excitatory · Role: Memory, attentiveness, sleep

The most common mental health disorder; 50% go undiagnosed because the right questions aren't asked. Ask: "Within the last 2 weeks, have you experienced…" SIG-E-CAPS: Sleep · Interest (anhedonia) · Guilt (worthlessness) · Energy · Concentration · Appetite ·…
Tool: PHQ-2 · Use: Prescreening · Population: ≥12 · Items: 2
Tool: PHQ-9 · Use: Screening, monitoring treatment · Population: ≥12; cognitive impairment; nursing home · Items: 9
Tool: Geriatric Depression Scale · Use: Screening · Population: ≥60; cognitive impairment · Items: 5, 15 or 30
Tool: Beck Depression Inventory · Use: Screening, monitoring · Population: 13–80 · Items: 21

All have similar sensitivity and specificity. History: prior episodes and treatment; family history (30–40% genetic); stressors, social, occupation (60–70% situational); psychiatric comorbidities that confound (bipolar, anxiety, alcohol/drug use); medical…

DSM-5-TR MDD: symptoms ≥2 weeks; anhedonia or depressed mood must be present; ≥5 symptoms most of the day nearly every day; distress; no other cause; no mania/hypomania. "Other specified depressive disorder" = clinically significant but below MDD criteria.

Labs — consider secondary causes in older patients, first episode, severe onset, or no clear precipitant: standard CBC, CMP, TSH; older adults FBG, B12, folate; impaired nutrition B12, folate; fertile females pregnancy test; suspected substance use urine drug…
PHQ-9: 0–4 · Severity: Minimal · Plan: Monitor; may not need treatment
PHQ-9: 5–9 · Severity: Mild · Plan: Offer treatment; clinical judgment and shared decision-making
PHQ-9: 15–19 · Severity: Moderately severe · Plan: Active treatment: psychotherapy, medication or both
Treatment: shared decision-making; depression-focused psychotherapy/CBT; generally a second-generation antidepressant (SSRI or SNRI); bupropion (NDRI) and serotonin modulators also effective.
SSRI choice: Less CYP450 effect (fewer interactions) · Drugs: Sertraline (Zoloft), citalopram (Celexa), escitalopram (Lexapro)
SSRI choice: More CYP450 effect · Drugs: Fluoxetine (Prozac), paroxetine (Paxil), fluvoxamine (Luvox)
SSRI side effect: Nausea · Notes: Most common; all SSRIs · Pearl: Start low, go slow
SSRI side effect: Diarrhea · Notes: Sertraline
SSRI side effect: Constipation · Notes: Paroxetine
SSRI side effect: Sexual dysfunction · Notes: Ejaculatory change, ↓libido, anorgasmia; paroxetine most · Pearl: Lower dose, add bupropion, switch to non-serotonergic drug or fluvoxamine
SSRI side effect: Somnolence · Notes: Paroxetine, citalopram, fluvoxamine · Pearl: Take at bedtime
SSRI side effect: Insomnia · Notes: Fluoxetine, sertraline · Pearl: Take in the AM
SSRI side effect: Weight gain · Notes: Paroxetine, escitalopram, citalopram; ~6 months · Pearl: Diet, exercise; fluoxetine least

Pregnancy: generally safe; escitalopram or sertraline preferred; avoid paroxetine; discuss risks/benefits. Lactation: low levels in milk; continue the pregnancy SSRI. Weigh risks of untreated depression.
Exclude bipolar disorder before an SSRI. Major depression may be its presenting symptom. Screen with the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (15 items; sensitivity 58%, specificity 93%).

Mania: Excess energy, grandiosity, fast speech, distractibility, agitation, hallucinations, impulsivity; substance misuse, legal and relationship problems common · Hypomania: Like mania but not severe enough to impair function; productive goal-directed…
Bipolar I: ≥1 manic episode (major depression less likely). Bipolar II: ≥1 hypomanic episode, ≥1 major depressive episode, no mania. If suspected: do NOT start antidepressants — refer.
Dosing: start low, go slow, don't stop, be patient (sertraline usual 50–200 mg; older adult start 25 mg).
Age: Young–middle adult · Expect improvement: 2–4 weeks · Expect relief: 6–12 weeks
Age: Older adult · Expect improvement: 4–6 weeks · Expect relief: 12–16 weeks
First episode: continue ≥6 months after remission.
SNRI: Duloxetine (Cymbalta) · Indications / considerations: MDD, GAD, fibromyalgia, neuropathy, chronic MSK pain; least likely to raise BP
SNRI: Venlafaxine (Effexor) · Indications / considerations: MDD, social anxiety, cataplexy; caution with bleeding risk
SNRI: Desvenlafaxine (Pristiq) · Indications / considerations: MDD; less sexual dysfunction
SNRI: Milnacipran (Savella) · Indications / considerations: Fibromyalgia; may ↑LFTs; avoid in ESRD
SNRI: Levomilnacipran (Fetzima) · Indications / considerations: MDD; avoid in ESRD
SNRI side effects: nausea, dizziness, diaphoresis, ↑BP (except duloxetine), sexual dysfunction, bleeding, hyponatremia.

Bupropion (NDRI, Wellbutrin): MDD, seasonal affective disorder, smoking cessation (Zyban), ADHD (off-label); with naltrexone (Contrave) for weight loss. CI: seizures, uncontrolled HTN. Monitor BP. AEs: dry mouth, nausea, insomnia, anxiety. No sexual side…

Discontinuation syndrome — likely if stopped abruptly, tapered over only 2–7 days, switched to a drug with different PK, 3–4 doses skipped, or brand switched to generic. Symptoms: fatigue, headache, nausea, agitation/anxiety, dizziness, insomnia, flu-like…
Switching method: Immediate switch · How: Stop one, start the other · When: Similar MOA and half-life
Switching method: Cross-taper · How: Taper old while increasing new, 1–2 weeks · When: Usual approach
Switching method: Washout · How: Taper, wait 5 half-lives, then start · When: Significant interactions (e.g., MAOIs)

Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity): from combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, St. John's wort, dextromethorphan, tramadol, TCAs, cyclobenzaprine). ↑BP, HR, temperature; confusion, restlessness, agitation; headache, muscle rigidity, N/V, tremor,…

All antidepressants carry an FDA boxed warning for increased suicidality, reported most in ages 18–24, at initiation and in the first 1–2 months. Efficacy studies: no change in suicide deaths; starting an antidepressant does not cause new-onset ideation;…

Risk factors: psychiatric disorder, hopelessness, impulsivity, isolation, prior attempts, family history, substance use, prolonged stress, abuse/neglect/trauma. Highest risk: never married; male (4:1); age 75+; firearms are the most common method. 988 Suicide…
Anxiety becomes pathologic when its intensity is disproportionate to the trigger.
Diagnosis: Depression · Worry: About past events · Screening tool: PHQ-9
Diagnosis: Generalized anxiety disorder · Worry: About future events · Screening tool: GAD-7
Diagnosis: Panic disorder · Worry: Paroxysmal, minutes to an hour; worry about future attacks · Screening tool: PADIS
Diagnosis: Social anxiety disorder · Worry: Intense, irrational fear of a specific object, situation or activity · Screening tool: SIAS-6, SPS-6

Masquerading diseases: Angina, arrhythmia, MI; anemia; hyperthyroidism; hypoglycemia; essential tremor; asthma, COPD, PE; carcinoid tumor · Masquerading drugs: Caffeine, cocaine; pseudoephedrine; theophylline; benzodiazepine or alcohol withdrawal;…

GAD (DSM-5-TR): excessive worry more days than not for ≥6 months; significant distress/impairment; ≥3 of: restlessness, muscle tension, irritability, impaired concentration, easy fatigue, sleep disturbance; not due to substances or another diagnosis.

GAD management: shared decision-making by severity and impact; CBT or psychotherapy. First-line SSRIs and SNRIs. Short-term PRN bridge by patient characteristics: benzodiazepines or hydroxyzine (nonaddictive). Adjunct: buspirone (add-on to SSRI/SNRI, daily…
Marked cognitive, affective and/or behavioral disruption in response to trauma.
Criterion: A: Traumatic event · Features: Threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence — experienced, witnessed or learned of; repeated/extreme exposure (first responders, military)
Criterion: B: Intrusion (≥1) · Features: Intrusive memories, distressing dreams, flashbacks, intense reactions to cues
Criterion: C: Avoidance · Features: Avoiding stimuli associated with the event

Criterion: D: Negative cognition and mood (≥2) · Features: Dissociative amnesia; exaggerated negative beliefs ("I am bad," "No one can be trusted"); persistent negative state, detachment; inability to feel positive emotions
Criterion: E: Arousal and reactivity · Features: Irritability/aggression, reckless behavior, on edge, sleep disturbance, hypervigilance; began after the event
First-line: trauma-focused psychotherapy; refer for psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy as indicated.

Substances (by social acceptability): caffeine, tobacco/nicotine, alcohol, prescription drugs (opioids, stimulants, gabapentin), marijuana, illicit drugs (cocaine, heroin, hallucinogens, inhalants). Assess: ever used, pattern, last use, frequency;…
Substance: Alcohol · Tool: Single item · Characteristics: "How many times in the past year have you had 5 (men) / 4 (women) or more drinks in a day?"
Substance: Alcohol · Tool: AUDIT-C · Characteristics: 3 items
Substance: Opioid · Tool: OWLS (overuse, worrying, losing interest, slowed/sedated) · Characteristics: 4 items, primary care
Substance: Opioid · Tool: RODS (Rapid Opioid Dependence Screen) · Characteristics: 8 items, dependence
Substance: Opioid · Tool: Opioid Risk Tool · Characteristics: Risk; complete before prescribing; self-report
Substance: Multiple · Tool: TAPS-1 / TAPS-2 · Characteristics: TAPS-1 4 items; TAPS-2 if positive

DSM-5-TR SUD: ≥2 in 12 months — larger amounts or longer than intended; can't cut down; excessive time obtaining/using/recovering; craving; failing major role obligations; use despite interpersonal problems; giving up activities; use in hazardous situations;…

Predominantly inattentive: Careless/poor attention to detail; short attention span; poor listening; lacks follow-through; disorganized; avoids concentration tasks; loses things; distracted; forgetful · Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive: Fidgets; trouble…
Combined presentation = both. Rating scales: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (WHO), Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scale, Wender Utah. Assess comorbidities, substance use, age of onset.
DSM-5 (children and adults): symptoms before age 12; >6 months; in ≥2 settings; interfere with functioning. <17 years: 6 symptoms per domain; ≥17 years: ≥5.

Management: CBT + medication preferred. First-line stimulants — amphetamines (Adderall), methylphenidate (Ritalin). Common AEs: weight loss, headache, insomnia, dry mouth, irritability, dysphoria; rare: priapism, ↑BP, tics. Alternatives: atomoxetine…

Always consult the Beers Criteria for older adults. OTC aids: antihistamines (diphenhydramine, doxylamine) block histamine receptors; melatonin regulates the sleep–wake cycle; herbals (valerian, chamomile, lavender) may calm.

Class: Benzodiazepines · Drugs: Temazepam (Restoril), lorazepam (Ativan), triazolam (Halcion) · Characteristics: Drowsiness, confusion, anterograde amnesia, next-day impairment; dependence/tolerance. CI: angle-closure glaucoma

Class: Z-drugs · Drugs: Zolpidem (Ambien), eszopiclone (Lunesta), zaleplon (Sonata) · Characteristics: Daytime drowsiness, dizziness, headache, complex sleep behaviors (sleepwalking), rebound insomnia. CI: prior complex sleep behaviors on the class
Class: Melatonin agonists · Drugs: Ramelteon (Rozerem), tasimelteon (Hetlioz), melatonin · Characteristics: Rare headache, dizziness, drowsiness
Class: TCA · Drugs: Doxepin (Silenor) · Characteristics: Anticholinergic; FDA-approved for insomnia, low dependence

Class: DORAs · Drugs: Suvorexant (Belsomra), lemborexant (Dayvigo), daridorexant (Quviviq) · Characteristics: Headache, drowsiness, dizziness, nausea; rare abnormal dreams, anxiety, mood change, suicidal thoughts
Q1. 70-year-old with foggy thoughts, poor concentration and appetite, no energy to be around people — next step: (1) TSH, B12, folate (2) screen with PHQ-9 (3) UA for UTI (4) CMP, CBC, TSH.

Q3. Must exclude before prescribing fluoxetine for MDD: (1) OCD (2) panic disorder (3) bipolar disorder (4) GAD.
Q4. Sertraline starting dose for a 75-year-old: (1) 25 mg (2) 50 mg (3) 75 mg (4) 100 mg.
Q5. First episode MDD after spouse's death, doesn't want long-term medication: (1) lifelong (2) 3 years (3) at least 1 year (4) at least 6 months after remission.
Q6. Partial response to citalopram after prior sertraline (PHQ-9 16 → 14): (1) switch to fluoxetine (2) sertraline + olanzapine (3) amitriptyline (4) switch to desvenlafaxine.
Q7. Herb dangerous with SSRIs: (1) ginkgo (2) St. John's wort (3) milk thistle (4) black cohosh.
Q8. First-line PTSD treatment: (1) trauma-focused psychotherapy (2) stress inoculation (3) ECT (4) serotonin-modulating drugs.
Q9. Contraindicates a stimulant for adult ADHD now: (1) depression (2) anxiety (3) active substance use disorder (4) controlled HTN.

"The abdomen is a poor historian" — build a good differential. Exam checklist: abdominal pain differentials, GERD, diarrhea, encopresis, GI red flags, hepatitis, IBS vs IBD, diverticulitis, fatty liver, labs and imaging.
History is critical: where, when, associated symptoms (nausea, vomiting, bowel movement), what relieves it. Pain may be intra- or extra-abdominal.
Location: Epigastric · Abdominal differential: Pancreatitis, gastric ulcer/gastritis, GERD, hepatobiliary · Extra-abdominal: Cardiac, pulmonary, vascular
Location: RUQ · Abdominal differential: Cholecystitis, acute hepatitis, other hepatobiliary · Extra-abdominal: Cardiac, pulmonary
Location: LUQ · Abdominal differential: Pancreatitis, PUD, GERD, gastritis, splenic · Extra-abdominal: Cardiac, vascular
Location: RLQ · Abdominal differential: Appendicitis, nephrolithiasis, diverticulitis, IBS, IBD, pyelonephritis · Extra-abdominal: Vascular, gynecologic, MSK
Location: LLQ · Abdominal differential: Appendicitis, diverticulitis, nephrolithiasis, pyelonephritis, IBD, IBS, colorectal cancer · Extra-abdominal: Vascular, gynecologic, MSK

Acute: gallbladder inflammation, usually gallstones (acalculous 5–10%). Steady, severe RUQ pain, sometimes colicky, epigastric or radiating to the right shoulder; triggered by a high-fat meal; fever; worse with movement. Murphy's sign = inspiratory arrest on…

Chronic (gallbladder dyskinesia, biliary colic): smoldering course alternating with acute colic; may lead to acute cholecystitis. Risk factors: female, obesity, pregnancy, advancing age. Imaging: ultrasound; cholescintigraphy (HIDA).
Sign: McBurney's · Technique: Deep tenderness at McBurney's point (⅔ from navel to right ASIS)
Sign: Obturator · Technique: Flex knee, internally rotate hip
Sign: Psoas · Technique: Lie on left side, extend hip
Sign: Markle's (heel drop/jar) · Technique: Stand on toes, drop suddenly onto heels

Retrograde flow of gastric contents into the esophagus: poor esophageal motility, dysfunctional LES, increased gastric volume and pressure. Reflux can be physiologic or pathologic. Presumptive diagnosis: pathologic symptoms ≥2 days/week without alarm…
Alarm symptoms — REFER: new onset at ≥60; GI bleeding or new IDA; anorexia/weight loss; dysphagia/odynophagia; vomiting (obstruction); GI cancer in a first-degree relative.
Class: Antacids (PRN) · Examples: Maalox, Mylanta, Rolaids, Tums · Action: ↑pH 20–30 min; fastest relief
Class: H2 receptor antagonists · Examples: Cimetidine (Tagamet), famotidine (Pepcid), nizatidine · Action: ↓acid 6–12 h; relief in ~60 min

Class: PPIs · Examples: Omeprazole (Prilosec), lansoprazole (Prevacid), rabeprazole (Aciphex), esomeprazole (Nexium), pantoprazole (Protonix) · Action: ↓acid secretion; relief in 1–3 days; 8-week trial
No relief after 8 weeks of a PPI → refer. Resolved after 8 weeks → stop and see whether symptoms recur in 2–4 weeks.

Barrett's esophagus — esophageal dysplasia from chronic GERD. Risk factors: male; age ≥50; non-Hispanic White; GERD ≥5–10 years; smoking; hiatal hernia; Barrett's or esophageal cancer in a first-degree relative.

Diverticulosis = sac-like protrusions of the bowel wall; 70–80% asymptomatic. Complications: diverticular bleeding (5–15%), diverticulitis (4–15%), abscess, fistula, obstruction, perforation. Classic diverticulitis: LLQ pain, nausea, low-grade fever,…

ACP 2021 outpatient management: antibiotics selectively, not routinely; pain control; liquid diet advanced as tolerated over 2–3 days; no repeat imaging if improving; colonoscopy in 6–8 weeks if none in the past year.

Crampy pain of varying location and character; stool varies (normal, diarrhea, constipation) with mucus; GERD symptoms, early satiety, nausea, chest pain. Serotonin-mediated (90% of serotonin is in the gut).
IBS type: All · First-line: Lifestyle: sleep, exercise, stress reduction, low-FODMAP diet
IBS type: Diarrhea · First-line: Loperamide · Second-line: Eluxadoline (Viberzi), rifaximin (Xifaxan)
IBS type: Constipation · First-line: Osmotic laxatives · Second-line: Lubiprostone (Amitiza), linaclotide (Linzess), plecanatide (Trulance)
IBS type: Either/mixed with persistent pain or psychologic symptoms · First-line: TCAs or SSRIs (add or switch)
Tip: abdominal pain and cramping → antispasmodic.

Wide differential: infectious, colitis, IBS, IBD (UC, Crohn), many more — get a good history (duration, frequency, associated symptoms). Small bowel: watery, large volume, cramping, bloating/gas. Large bowel: frequent, regular, small volume; fever, mucus,…
Infectious: Viral (most common) · Organisms: Norovirus, rotavirus · Suspect when: Self-limited
Infectious: Bacterial · Organisms: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, C. difficile, Staphylococcus · Suspect when: Immunocompromised or severe illness >1 week
Infectious: Parasitic · Organisms: Giardia · Suspect when: Immunocompromised, international travel, poor sanitation
Red flags: rectal bleeding; nocturnal BMs; nocturnal or progressive pain; weight loss; anemia, ↑inflammatory markers, electrolyte disturbance.
Symptom: Anal pain with defecation · Differential: Anal fissure, rectal carcinoma
Symptom: Night sweats, fever, weight loss · Differential: Malignancy, chronic infection or inflammation
Symptom: Diarrhea preceding or with blood · Differential: Colitis
Symptom: Change in stool frequency or caliber · Differential: Malignancy
IBD (UC, Crohn): peak 15–30 years; diarrhea, bloody stools, pain, tenesmus, fatigue, anemia, sometimes weight loss. Recognize and refer to GI.

Second leading cause of cancer death in males, third in females. 86% diagnosed before 50 are symptomatic with advanced disease and poor prognosis. Most arise from adenomatous polyps (⅔ of polyps): polyp → dysplasia → cancer over ≥10 years. Average-risk…
Method: Guaiac FOBT · Frequency: Annually, 3 specimens · Comments: Guaiac-based
Method: FIT · Frequency: Annually, 1 specimen · Comments: More sensitive than gFOBT
Method: FIT-DNA (Cologuard) · Frequency: Every 1–3 years · Comments: ↑sensitivity, ↓specificity; average risk only
Method: Colonoscopy · Frequency: Every 10 years · Comments: Gold standard
Method: Flexible sigmoidoscopy · Frequency: Every 5 years · Comments: Only to the splenic flexure
Metabolism/conversion: ALT, AST. Synthetic: bile, albumin, PT. Excretory: bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase.
Elevation: ALT and AST · Consider: Liver injury, hepatitis, MAFLD; acute liver failure if >10× ULN
Elevation: ALP · Consider: Bone disease, liver disease, obstructed bile ducts
Elevation: Bilirubin · Consider: RBC destruction, liver disease, bile duct obstruction, Gilbert
Elevation: PT/INR · Consider: Cirrhosis, primary liver cancer (with abnormal LFTs)
Elevation: Albumin · Consider: Usually normal in liver disease
Affects ⅓ of the US population and ⅔ of people with diabetes; associated with ASCVD, kidney disease, diabetes.
Identify at-risk patients: ≥2 metabolic syndrome risk factors, type 2 DM, steatosis on imaging, or ↑ALT/AST.
History and labs: heavy alcohol use; CBC, LFTs, hepatitis panel.
Noninvasive testing: FIB-4 score (age, AST/ALT, platelets).
FIB-4: <1.3 (low risk) · Management: Primary care: physical activity, diet, alcohol avoidance; weight loss >7–10%; CVD risk reduction; diabetes per ADA
FIB-4: >1.3 · Management: Refer to hepatology (biopsy and/or pharmacologic management likely)
ALT > AST. Five agents (A–E); B, C and D can become chronic.
Type: Hepatitis A · Screening: No universal recommendation; by risk (occupational, travel, homelessness, MSM, injection drug use)
Type: Hepatitis B · Screening: One-time universal ≥18 unless immune; each pregnancy
Type: Hepatitis C · Screening: One-time universal ≥18; each pregnancy; annually if high-risk (IV drug use)
IgM = "minute" (first antibody in acute infection); IgG = "gone" (immunity, usually after infection resolves).
Hepatitis A: Anti-HAV IgG + · Interpretation: Immune
Hepatitis A: Anti-HAV IgM + · Interpretation: Acute infection
Hepatitis A: Both negative · Interpretation: No immunity — immunize
Hepatitis B marker: HBsAg · Meaning: Infected (currently or past)
Hepatitis B marker: Anti-HBs · Meaning: Immune (vaccine or recovery)
Hepatitis B marker: Anti-HBc (total) · Meaning: Current or previous infection
Hepatitis B marker: IgM anti-HBc · Meaning: Acute hepatitis B (≤6 months)
HBsAg: − · Anti-HBc: − · Anti-HBs: − · IgM anti-HBc: NA · Interpretation: Susceptible — needs vaccine
HBsAg: − · Anti-HBc: + · Anti-HBs: + · IgM anti-HBc: NA · Interpretation: Immune from resolved infection
HBsAg: − · Anti-HBc: − · Anti-HBs: + · IgM anti-HBc: NA · Interpretation: Immune from vaccination
HBsAg: + · Anti-HBc: + · Anti-HBs: − · IgM anti-HBc: + · Interpretation: Acutely infected
HBsAg: + · Anti-HBc: + · Anti-HBs: − · IgM anti-HBc: − · Interpretation: Chronically infected
HBsAg: − · Anti-HBc: + · Anti-HBs: − · IgM anti-HBc: − · Interpretation: Unclear: resolved infection (most common), false-positive anti-HBc, low-level chronic, or resolving acute

Hepatitis B quick list: Infection = +surface antigen and +core — IgM negative = chronic, IgM positive = acute. Immunity = +surface antibody — core positive = from infection, core negative = from vaccination.
HCV testing: screen with HCV antibody → nonreactive = no HCV infection; reactive → HCV RNA → detected = current infection; not detected = no current infection.
Study: Plain flat/upright abdomen · Use: Ileus, obstruction, perforation · Comments: Quick, cheap, available
Study: Abdominal ultrasound · Use: Gallbladder, pelvic organs, appendix (peds), kidneys, liver · Comments: Hard with high BMI; noninvasive; no radiation
Study: CT · Use: Acute abdominal pain, diverticulitis · Comments: Oral contrast for GI tract; IV contrast for vasculature
Study: MRI · Use: Hepatocellular carcinoma, metastases · Comments: Not for acute setting
Study: HIDA · Use: Rule out cholecystitis · Comments: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid
Study: EGD · Use: Upper GI · Comments: Invasive, anesthesia
Study: Colonoscopy · Use: Lower GI · Comments: Invasive, bowel prep, anesthesia

Functional problems: hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism (primary, subclinical, secondary). Structural problems: goiter (enlargement), thyroiditis (inflammation), nodules (benign, toxic, cancer). Structural problems can cause functional problems.

TSH (anterior pituitary) stimulates thyroid hormone production. It is the most sensitive measure of thyroid function — the "early warning system": it changes before T3/T4, is more reliable, and a small change in T3/T4 produces a large change in TSH. Used to…
T4 (thyroxine): 4 iodine atoms, 80% released by thyroid; free T4 is active (99.5% bound/inactive); more specific to hypothyroidism.
T3 (triiodothyronine): 3 iodine atoms; 20% from thyroid, most converted from T4 peripherally; more specific to hyperthyroidism.
Negative feedback: ↓T3/T4 → hypothalamus TRH → anterior pituitary TSH → thyroid T3/T4 → levels restored.

Feature: Morning stiffness · Osteoarthritis (OA): ≤60 min · Rheumatoid arthritis (RA): >60 min

The scaphoid stabilizes the midcarpal joint and gets its blood supply from the radial artery. It is the most commonly injured wrist bone, usually from a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH).
Signs of fracture are deep, dull wrist pain that is worse with gripping or squeezing, and anatomic snuffbox tenderness. Scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis.
Step: Imaging · Details: PA, lateral, oblique and scaphoid-view radiographs. If negative, get MRI or CT. If MRI isn't available, repeat radiographs in 7–14 days.
Step: Immobilize · Details: Suspected fracture not confirmed on radiograph. Confirmed fracture on radiograph or MRI: immobilization up to 5 months.
Step: Ortho referral · Details: Any confirmed fracture (displaced or not), delayed presentation (>3 weeks), carpal instability

Tip: Initial imaging can be falsely negative. When you're suspicious, immobilize, repeat the imaging and refer. A missed scaphoid fracture can lead to avascular necrosis, with chronic pain, deformity and disability.

The pain is worse with movement
Numbness of the buttocks and perineum
The pain is colicky and radiates to the flank

A 30-year-old patient presents with knee pain after a fall 24 hours ago. There is diffuse tenderness and mild swelling of the knee. The patient can walk in the office with minimal difficulty. How should this patient be managed?
An adult presents with right ankle pain after an injury earlier this morning. According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, a radiograph is indicated if the patient:
is unable to bear weight for 10 steps
has tenderness only in the malleolar zone
was able to bear weight immediately after the injury
Unable to bear weight for 4 steps.
A patient presents with their third acute gout flare within 12 months. In addition to lifestyle changes, the best management plan is to prescribe:
Dermis: handles tensile load and contains nerves
Hypodermis: insulation, energy and fluid storage
Term: Abscess · Definition: Deep infection; a localized collection of pus
Term: Furuncle (boil) · Definition: Deep infection of a hair follicle
Term: Bulla (blister) · Definition: Fluid- or pus-filled lesion >0.5 cm
Term: Macule · Definition: Flat change in skin color (brown, blue, red or hypopigmented)
Term: Nodule · Definition: Solid lesion >0.5–2.0 cm; over 2.0 cm it is a tumor
Term: Papule · Definition: Raised, solid lesion ≤0.5 cm; color varies
Term: Plaque · Definition: Raised, solid lesion >0.5 cm
Term: Vesicle · Definition: Elevated, fluid-containing lesion ≤0.5 cm
Term: Wheal (hive) · Definition: Transient, rounded or flat-topped plaque
Know the anatomy: which layer is affected? Take an OLD CARTS history.
Use pattern recognition on exam: texture, plane, depth, color, borders, shape, blanching and distribution.
Ask whether this is a skin problem or a systemic problem.
Tip: Document a detailed description so other clinicians can "see" the lesion from your notes.
Choose the route: topical, or systemic (oral or IV).
Supportive care is enough for some conditions; not every condition needs medication.
When unsure: "If it's wet, make it dry. If it's dry, make it wet."
Bacteria: gram-positive organisms, usually Staph or Strep
Fungi, two main types: dermatophytes (tinea) and Candida. Tinea versicolor is caused by a yeast.
Viruses: herpes, HPV, molluscum contagiosum, HIV, plantar warts, varicella, viral exanthems
Impetigo is a superficial infection caused by Streptococcus, Staphylococcus or both. The classic description is "honey-colored crusts", often around the mouth. Treat topically.
Ecthyma is the deep, ulcerative form of impetigo and needs oral antibiotics.
Cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the dermis and hypodermis, caused by group A Streptococcus and Staph aureus.
Signs: erythema with poorly circumscribed margins, edema, tenderness, warmth; possibly fever and elevated WBC.
Nonpurulent cellulitis: oral dicloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin/clavulanate or clindamycin.
Tip: Deep, nonpurulent infection plus systemic symptoms means systemic antibiotics.
Abscess. In a student athlete with a 2-cm abscess, think MRSA. The treatment is incision and drainage.
Tip: "When there's pus about, let it out!"

Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, superficial or deep. It presents as pustules and/or papules at the follicles. It is usually Staph (sometimes Strep pyogenes). Recent hot tub use: think Pseudomonas.
Bacterial skin infections: treatment per IDSA
Infection: Cellulitis without purulence · Usual organism: MSSA, Strep · Treatment: Cephalexin, cefadroxil, clindamycin
Infection: Cellulitis with purulence · Usual organism: MRSA · Treatment: I&D first-line; TMP-SMX, clindamycin, tetracycline, linezolid (5–10 days)

Infection: Carbuncle (deep furuncle/boil) and abscess · Usual organism: Staph (MRSA) · Treatment: I&D first-line. Antibiotics if fever, cellulitis >2.5 cm, systemic symptoms or failed initial treatment
Infection: Impetigo (superficial) · Usual organism: Strep, MSSA or both · Treatment: Mupirocin (Bactroban) or retapamulin (Altabax) BID × 5 days
Infection: Ecthyma (deep, ulcerative impetigo) · Usual organism: MSSA (most common), MRSA, Strep · Treatment: MSSA: dicloxacillin, cephalexin. MRSA: doxycycline, clindamycin or TMP-SMX
Infection: Folliculitis · Usual organism: MSSA · Treatment: Topical: mupirocin or clindamycin gel. Oral: cephalexin, dicloxacillin QID. MRSA: doxycycline or TMP-SMX. Pseudomonas: ciprofloxacin
Bites can lead to bacterial infection from two sources:
The biter's oral flora. Dog or cat: Pasteurella. Human: Staph, Strep, anaerobes.
The patient's skin flora: Staph and Strep are most common.
The antibiotic of choice is amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin).
Antibiotic prophylaxis with amoxicillin/clavulanate for 3–5 days if any of these apply:
Involvement of bones, joints, hands, face or genitals
Tetanus prophylaxis if the last dose was more than 5 years ago.
High-risk animals: skunks, raccoons, foxes, bats
The animal can't be obtained for testing
Refer emergently for rabies immune globulin (HRIG) and the multidose rabies vaccine series. Rabies is a reportable condition.
Organism · Dermatophyte (tinea): Filamentous fungi · Candida: Yeast
Look · Dermatophyte (tinea): Pruritic, scaling border, spreads centrifugally, central clearing · Candida: Pruritic, erythematous base, white patches, burning, satellite lesions
Named by location · Dermatophyte (tinea): Capitis (scalp/hair), corporis (body), cruris (groin), unguium (nails) · Candida: Oropharyngeal, vaginitis, balanitis, invasive
Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) needs oral therapy, not a topical antifungal.
Differential for a scaly, circumscribed, erythematous truncal lesion with central clearing: tinea corporis, eczema, the herald patch of pityriasis rosea. Cellulitis does not fit.
Viral exanthems are characteristic skin lesions of viral illness (measles, rubella, varicella).
Viral enanthems are oral eruptions before, with or after an exanthem, such as Koplik spots in measles.
Sexually transmitted: HPV (genital warts), genital HSV, HIV (acute exanthem and infectious or neoplastic conditions).
Zoster presents as painful, clustered vesicles in a dermatomal distribution (e.g., T4 across the chest) that do not cross the midline. It is very painful and has a prodrome.
Pain: NSAIDs for mild to moderate pain, opioids for severe pain.
<72 hours from onset: oral acyclovir, famciclovir, valacyclovir (or brivudine) for 7 days.
>72 hours: treat only if new lesions are still appearing or the patient is immunocompromised.
Tip: If the patient is immunocompromised, ALWAYS prescribe antivirals, regardless of time since onset.
Complication: Ramsay Hunt syndrome · Symptoms / management: Ear pain, vesicles in the ear, ipsilateral facial paralysis. Refer to ENT.
Complication: Postherpetic neuralgia · Symptoms / management: Pain lasting more than 4 months in the same dermatome
Complication: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus · Symptoms / management: Refer to ophthalmology urgently
Complication: Meningitis / encephalitis · Symptoms / management: Send to the ED
Shingrix (recombinant zoster vaccine, RZV), per CDC:
2 IM doses, 2–6 months apart. Immunocompromised patients may get them 1–2 months apart.
It is a recombinant (not live) vaccine, safer and more effective than Zostavax (live). Give it regardless of Zostavax history.
Give it after the acute episode resolves.

Spiders. Bites inject toxins that cause swelling and inflammation. Some (e.g., brown recluse) cause tissue necrosis or systemic neurologic symptoms. Typically there is a single lesion, and it doesn't affect several household members. A definitive diagnosis…
Tip: Spider bites are often mistaken for MRSA abscesses, herpes zoster or Lyme disease.
Symptoms appear 2–14 days after exposure. Transmission requires about 36 hours of attachment.
Lyme disease is transmitted most often. It causes erythema migrans ("bull's-eye" rash).
Other tick-borne diseases: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), with a diffuse rash that includes the palms and soles; babesiosis; ehrlichiosis.
Lyme treatment: Doxycycline 100 mg BID × 10 days, OR amoxicillin, OR cefuroxime · Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): Doxycycline 200 mg, single dose (peds: 4.4 mg/kg)
Lyme treatment: Doxycycline is the only recommended treatment for RMSF. · Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): PEP is not recommended for RMSF.
Doxycycline is safe for the patient
Bed bugs. Pruritic erythematous papules 2–5 mm. The reaction varies from immediate to 10 days later. Untreated, they resolve in about 1 week. Diagnosis requires finding the bed bugs.
Symptoms appear 3–6 weeks after exposure. Spread is skin to skin, not animal to human.
Intensely pruritic small erythematous papules with burrows.
Distribution: sides and webs of the fingers, wrists, axillae, areolae, genitalia, waist.
Treatment: topical permethrin cream. Safe for age >2 months and in pregnancy and lactation. Apply to the entire body (except the head) once; may repeat in 2 weeks.
Distribution: head (capitis, most common), body (corporis), pubic hair (pubis, sexually transmitted).
Treatment: topical permethrin or malathion. Wet combing with proper technique every 3–4 days for at least 3 weeks is a reasonable alternative.
The manual shows images of four dermatitis types. The descriptions below come from standard references:
Eczema (atopic dermatitis): pruritic, dry, erythematous patches, often flexural in older children and adults.
Psoriasis: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees).
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy, yellowish scale on the scalp (dandruff), eyebrows and nasolabial folds.
Contact dermatitis: erythema, often vesicular, sharply limited to the area of contact.
Potency is the amount of drug needed for an effect. It depends on the vasoconstriction produced, the immunosuppressive effects and the vehicle.
The vehicle is the medium that carries the drug.
Vehicle (most to least potent): Ointment · Use: Thick or hyperkeratotic lesions; avoid in hairy areas
Vehicle (most to least potent): Cream · Use: Less residue, dries quickly; skin folds and acute inflammation
Vehicle (most to least potent): Lotion · Use: Hairy areas; less occlusive, dries quickly
Vehicle (most to least potent): Gel · Use: Hairy areas, especially the scalp (nongreasy)
Vehicle (most to least potent): Foam · Use: Ideal for the scalp, but expensive
Benign: seborrheic keratosis, skin tags, polyps, cysts, lipoma, many others
Malignant: basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), melanoma
Asymmetry: one half doesn't match the other
Color: more than one color in the lesion
Refer lesions highly suspicious for malignancy. Do a punch or shave biopsy for lesions of uncertain cause with low suspicion of malignancy.

Seborrheic keratosis is a benign, brown, warty lesion with a "stuck-on" look, usually on the chest, back or scalp. It may get irritated and bleed. There may be one or many, often a cosmetic concern. Treat symptomatic lesions with cryotherapy, curettage/shave…
Actinic (solar) keratosis is a precancerous scaling macule, papule or plaque in sun-exposed areas. It may progress to SCC, and there's no way to predict which will.
Treatment: destructive therapy (liquid nitrogen cryosurgery, shave excision) or topicals (5-fluorouracil, imiquimod).
Refer for biopsy if indurated; painful, ulcerated or bleeding; or hyperkeratotic/hypertrophic and not resolving or recurring after standard therapy.

Cancer: Basal cell carcinoma · Features: Pearly pink-red or flesh-colored nodule with telangiectasia; may be scaly. Painless. Shoulders, chest, face, back. Light skin, sun exposure, tanning beds, genetics.
Cancer: Squamous cell carcinoma · Features: Variable: plaque, crusting, ulceration, bleeding; flesh-toned to erythematous. Face, neck, scalp, extremities. Risks: sun exposure, actinic keratosis.

Cancer: Melanoma · Features: The "ugly duckling" lesion that differs from the patient's other nevi. Violates ABCDE, especially if changing or >6 mm. Sensory change, itch or inflammation. Legs, upper back, sun-exposed areas. Brown/black longitudinal streak in…
A suspicious pigmented lesion is referred for excisional biopsy first. Don't punch-biopsy it or freeze it in the office.
SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease, more common in Black, Asian and Hispanic women of childbearing age.

Manifestations: joint and muscle pain, fatigue, hair loss, thrombocytopenia, mouth sores, nervous system problems, lung or heart inflammation, abdominal pain, kidney involvement, skin rash, retinal problems, fever.
Malar ("butterfly") rash: an erythematous, maculopapular rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge, often brought on by sun exposure.
A positive ANA is the required entry criterion for the diagnostic criteria.
Erysipelas: a well-demarcated, bright red rash with raised edges in a toxic-looking patient, caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.
Necrotizing fasciitis: a rare, rapidly progressing infection with red or purple skin, pain out of proportion, fever and necrosis.
A severe mucocutaneous reaction with extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis, caused by a medication or infection.
Prodrome: fever >102°F (38.9°C) and flu-like symptoms for 1–3 days.
Lesions: target lesions with central dusky purpura, possibly bullae and blisters. They spread from the face downward and involve the mucous membranes.
A positive Nikolsky sign (skin exfoliates with rubbing) may be present.
Diseases that present with vesicles/bullae, papules/macules, pustules/purulence, nodules and plaques
Dermatologic emergencies; systemic conditions with skin signs
For each, know the presentation, diagnosis, differential, drug and non-drug management, follow-up, normal course and when to refer.

Topic: Narcotics · Detail: for severe pain

ARS is symptomatic inflammation of the paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary).
Causes: viruses (most common); bacteria (<2% of cases); fungi (rare); allergies; irritants; dry air; GERD.
Symptoms: Nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge · Physical exam: Sinus tenderness
Symptoms: Facial pain or pressure, worse bending forward · Physical exam: Mucosal erythema
Symptoms: Maxillary dental pain · Physical exam: Purulent posterior pharyngeal or nasal secretions
Symptoms: Fatigue, fever, cough · Physical exam: Air-fluid levels on transillumination
Course: symptoms peak on days 3–6 and resolve in 10–14 days.
Medication: Saline irrigation · Role in symptom relief: Recommended
Medication: Intranasal glucocorticoids · Role in symptom relief: Recommended
Medication: Mucolytics (guaifenesin) · Role in symptom relief: Thin secretions to help drainage
Medication: Topical and oral decongestants · Role in symptom relief: May help congestion
Medication: Antihistamines · Role in symptom relief: Not recommended: may overdry the mucosa. Consider if allergic rhinitis is present.
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) is a secondary bacterial infection. Suspect it with any of these patterns:
Severe: at onset and lasting at least 3 days (fever, purulent discharge, ill appearance)
Worsening, "double-sickening": symptoms improve, then worsen again
Pathogens: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Complications include orbital cellulitis and meningitis.
Recent antibiotic exposure: high-dose amoxicillin/clavulanate ER (2000/125 mg BID).
Penicillin allergy: doxycycline or a third-generation cephalosporin.
Allergic rhinitis is inflammation of the nasal mucous membranes.
Symptoms: sneezing, rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, congestion, nasal and mucosal itching, infraorbital edema (allergic shiners), allergic conjunctivitis.
Intranasal glucocorticoids (fluticasone, mometasone, beclomethasone): preferred monotherapy for persistent nasal and conjunctival symptoms.
Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine): better than oral antihistamines.
Second-generation oral antihistamines (fexofenadine, loratadine, cetirizine): less sedating than first-generation.
Intranasal decongestant (oxymetazoline): helps with severe congestion when given before the intranasal steroid or antihistamine.
Systemic corticosteroids: only for very severe or intractable symptoms.
Oral decongestants and leukotriene receptor antagonists: risks may outweigh benefits. Montelukast carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events, including suicidal thoughts.
Contraindicated: uncontrolled hypertension; MAOI therapy within 14 days.
Use caution with: closed-angle glaucoma, CAD, hyperthyroidism, urinary retention.
Misuse potential: stimulant use by athletes; illegal methamphetamine production.
Oxymetazoline (local): overuse causes rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion).
Anterior (90%): from Kiesselbach plexus, an anastomosis of five major arteries.
Posterior (5–10%): in older patients, hard to control. Refer to the ER.
Bleeding disorder, anticoagulation and hypertension, which raise the risk of a posterior or severe bleed
Refer if the patient is hemodynamically unstable or the bleed is severe (>30 min, or recurrent over 24 h).
Nasal compression: pinch the nose tightly for ≥5 minutes.
Cautery: with the bleed visualized, using a silver nitrate stick.
Viral: 50–80% of cases, usually common-cold viruses. Less often HIV, CMV, EBV.
Bacterial (less common): group A Streptococcus (GAS) and other respiratory bacteria.
Strep pharyngitis accounts for 5–15% of adult cases. The symptoms spell FLEA:
Criterion: Enlarged anterior cervical nodes · Points: 1
Criterion: Tonsillar exudate or swelling · Points: 1
Score: 0–2 · Risk: Low · Action: Testing not recommended
Score: 3 · Risk: Moderate · Action: Consider testing
Score: 4–5 · Risk: High · Action: Empiric antibiotics recommended; consider RADT or culture
Testing. A test is only as good as the sample.
Rapid antigen detection test (RADT): 70–90% sensitive, 90–100% specific.
First-line: penicillin (Pen G, Pen V or amoxicillin).
Type I (immediate) reaction: second- or third-generation cephalosporin with caution, or clindamycin.
Clarithromycin or azithromycin: check local GAS resistance rates first.
GAS complications: rheumatic fever, acute (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis, peritonsillar abscess. Periorbital cellulitis is not a GAS pharyngitis complication.
Epiglottitis is inflammation and edema of the epiglottis, classically from H. influenzae type b (Hib); also S. pneumoniae, S. aureus and others. It causes rapidly progressive airway obstruction.
The classic tetrad is fever, pharyngitis (sore throat), fatigue and posterior lymphadenopathy. Splenomegaly occurs in about 50%. Diagnosis can be made clinically.
Stage: Acute · Anti-VCA IgM: + · Anti-VCA IgG: + · EBNA: −
Stage: Acute or past · Anti-VCA IgM: − · Anti-VCA IgG: + · EBNA: +
Stage: Past · Anti-VCA IgM: − · Anti-VCA IgG: + · EBNA: +
Stage: Late primary or reactivation · Anti-VCA IgM: + · Anti-VCA IgG: + · EBNA: +
Anti-VCA IgM is present from onset to about 6 weeks.
Anti-VCA IgG appears in the acute phase and stays positive for life.
EBNA appears 2–4 months after onset and stays positive for life.
The Monospot test can give false negatives, especially early.
Facial and jaw pain differential: trigeminal neuralgia, TMJ dysfunction, acute rhinosinusitis, dental infection.
Tip: Consider a dental cause whenever a patient presents with facial or jaw pain.
Eustachian tube dysfunction. The eustachian tube equalizes air pressure between the atmosphere and the middle ear.
Obstructive symptoms: ear pain, muffled hearing, tinnitus, ear popping, imbalance.
Complications: otitis media with effusion (OME), retracted eardrum, chronic otitis media.
Treatment: treat the underlying cause, such as allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis or reflux.
Condition: Otitis media with effusion · Key points: Noninfected fluid from eustachian tube dysfunction. Muffled hearing, fullness, ear pain. Usually self-limited.

Condition: Acute otitis media · Key points: May follow OME. Ear pain, hearing loss, pressure, dizziness, bulging TM, often after a URI. Organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Amoxicillin first-line.
Condition: TM rupture · Key points: From barotrauma, a foreign body, or blunt or noise trauma. Sudden ear pain, hearing loss, bloody otorrhea, vertigo, tinnitus. Usually heals on its own.
Tragal tenderness and a narrow, inflamed canal: otitis externa
Severe ear pain, otorrhea, hearing loss and mastoid tenderness: mastoiditis
Ear pain, mild hearing loss, bulging TM and a recent URI: acute otitis media
The USPSTF does not recommend universal hearing screening in adults.
The whisper test is useful for screening when the patient isn't aware of a loss.
Refer for audiometry for any complaint of hearing loss. It determines the type (conductive, sensorineural or mixed) and the severity.
In older adults, the most important reason to correct hearing loss is that it leads to understimulation, isolation and possible cognitive decline.
Site · Conductive: Outer or middle ear; sound can't pass through the canal or TM · Sensorineural: Cochlea, CN VIII or CNS

Causes · Conductive: Mostly obstruction: cerumen impaction, foreign body (including headphones), otitis externa, OME, eustachian tube dysfunction · Sensorineural: Presbycusis (most common): age-related, genetic plus noise exposure, with trouble hearing…
Weber (tuning fork on the skull) · Conductive: Louder in the affected ear · Sensorineural: Louder in the unaffected ear
Rinne (mastoid vs. air) · Conductive: Bone conduction louder than air (abnormal) · Sensorineural: Air louder than bone (normal pattern)
Lateralizes to the bad ear: do a Rinne. Bone louder than air means conductive loss.
Lateralizes to the good ear: sensorineural loss.
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, tinnitus, fluctuating hearing loss and aural fullness. Hearing loss may become permanent. The course is unpredictable, and Dix–Hallpike is for BPPV, not Ménière.
Auditory emergency. Refer to ENT or the ER for hearing loss that is abrupt, unexplained, unilateral and sensorineural.
Chalazion: painless lid swelling over weeks, without drainage or injection.
Uveitis or iritis: inflammation from infection, autoimmune disease or trauma
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: rapid rise in IOP
Keratitis: corneal inflammation from infection, injury or contact lenses
Red-eye history that needs ophthalmology: change in vision; foreign-body sensation with inability to keep the eye open; photophobia. A scratchy, gritty foreign-body sensation alone is less worrying.
Presentation: Bilateral mucoid discharge, nasal congestion, sneezing · Refer?: No · Likely diagnosis: Allergic or viral conjunctivitis
Presentation: Sudden severe pain, redness and blurred vision in the right eye · Refer?: Yes · Likely diagnosis: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Presentation: Flashes, floaters, then a "curtain" of peripheral vision loss · Refer?: Yes · Likely diagnosis: Retinal detachment
Presentation: Painless bright red pool of blood on the eye after coughing · Refer?: No · Likely diagnosis: Subconjunctival hemorrhage
Glaucoma. Closure of the anterior chamber angle raises IOP and causes optic neuropathy.
Open-angle: Most common · Angle-closure: Medical emergency
Open-angle: Develops gradually; asymptomatic early · Angle-closure: Sudden severe eye pain, headache
Open-angle: Vision loss from optic nerve damage (peripheral first) · Angle-closure: Nausea and vomiting
Open-angle: Blindness if not treated early · Angle-closure: Blurred vision, halos around lights
Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of permanent vision loss in older adults.
Dry: gradual vision loss. Wet: rapid, severe vision loss.
Symptoms: central blind spot (scotoma) and curving of straight lines (Amsler grid). Peripheral and color vision stay normal.
Retinopathy is retinal damage from hypertension, diabetes, macular degeneration or genetic factors. Signs: cotton-wool spots, flame hemorrhages, hard exudates, AV nicking.
Eye pain. Refer emergently to the ER or ophthalmology unless noted.
Condition: Hyphema · Cause: Usually trauma; blood in the anterior chamber · Findings: Blood visible at the base of the iris; decreased visual acuity
Condition: Corneal abrasion · Cause: Trauma, contact lens wear · Findings: Foreign-body sensation, can't keep the eye open, defect on fluorescein staining. Specialty referral only if indicated.

Condition: Scleritis · Cause: Underlying rheumatologic or autoimmune disease · Findings: Diffusely injected, redder than conjunctivitis; headache; severe pain

Condition: Keratitis · Cause: Herpes virus; bacteria (Staph, Pseudomonas); overnight contact lens wear · Findings: Watery discharge, blurred vision, ciliary flush, dendritic lesions (herpes) on fluorescein or slit-lamp exam
