Tell normal aging from pathologic aging.
Effects of aging on organs: less tissue mass, fewer functional cells, reduced compliance, diminished perfusion and poorly coordinated systemic responses. These changes predispose to disease.
Normal (physiologic) aging follows a predictable pattern, but its rate and extent vary with genetics, lifestyle and environment.
Body rhythms change, affecting sleep, stress and digestion.
Presbyopia, presbycusis and mild word-finding difficulty are normal.
Pathologic aging is when normal aging processes speed up enough to cause disease.
Example: decreased gut motility and flora lead to anorexia and nutritional deficiency, which weakens the intestinal walls and leads to diverticulosis, constipation and bowel obstruction.
Disease is more debilitating than in younger adults.
Drugs may act differently and cause harm.

Manifestations: dementia, incontinence, dry mouth, atrial fibrillation, infection, ED, tooth decay, hypogonadism, blindness, dehydration, BPH, wounds, fractures, drug toxicity, liver failure, renal failure, burns, falls, constipation, diabetes, pneumonia,…

Goals of care are part of the assessment, especially in older adults. Ask what the patient knows about their health, what their goals and values are, and whether diagnosis and treatment should be pursued.
The goal is often to relieve suffering, whether the patient's or loved ones', and whether caused by the disease or the treatment.
Suffering is individual: pain, fear, debilitation, death, financial burden, loss of time.
Example: an older patient with Alzheimer dementia and a history of breast cancer presents with fatigue and weight loss. Discuss goals of care before ordering a workup.
Tools: POLST (state-specific), Serious Illness Conversation Guide, Best Case/Worst Case framework.
Advance care planning is billable. Document these conversations and formalize advance directives.
Advance care planning means documenting decisions before an emergency, such as CPR, mechanical ventilation, nutrition and hydration, and comfort care.

Life expectancy covers quantity and quality of life. It often must be estimated for guidelines, especially cancer screening. More disease means shorter life expectancy; life-expectancy tables can help.
Medicare is insurance for U.S. adults over 65.
Part A (hospital) and Part B (medical) are the core enrollment.
Patients then choose Part D (drugs) with or without supplemental insurance, or Part C (Medicare Advantage).
Initial Preventive Physical Exam (IPPE, "Welcome to Medicare")
Medical, social and family history, focused on risk factors, functional ability, safety and medications.
Exam: vitals, height, weight, and an exam suited to the history.
Preventive services: ECG once, age-appropriate screenings, covered preventive services.
E/M services can be added as needed.
Covers the 30 days after discharge from an inpatient setting to a community residence.
Medicare reimburses interactive contact and follow-up visits. Pay special attention to vulnerable older adults.
Advance care planning and goals of care
Screening for AAA, depression and alcohol use disorder
Tip: Documentation must support a service in order to bill it.
The level of prevention is guided by the goal of care.

Level: Primary · Memory word: Prevention · Purpose: Stop disease from occurring · Examples: Immunizations, exercise, seatbelts, fall prevention, handwashing, dental cleanings, healthy lifestyle (diet, exercise, sleep, community engagement, hobbies,…
Level: Secondary · Memory word: Screening · Purpose: Detect asymptomatic disease early · Examples: Mammogram, BP measurement, wellness exams, dental radiographs

Level: Tertiary · Memory word: Treatment · Purpose: Limit complications and progression · Examples: Smoking cessation in COPD, cardiac rehab after MI, support groups for terminal illness, lowering A1c in diabetes, PT after injury
Condition: Alcohol use disorder · Test: Questionnaire · Who: All adults · How often: —
Condition: Drug use disorder · Test: Questionnaire · Who: All adults · How often: —
Condition: Tobacco · Test: "Have you thought about quitting?" · Who: All adults who use tobacco · How often: Every visit
Condition: Hypertension · Test: BP measurement · Who: All adults · How often: Annually
Condition: AAA · Test: Abdominal ultrasound · Who: Men 65–75 who have ever smoked · How often: Once
Condition: Diabetes · Test: A1c, FPG or random glucose · Who: Adults 35–70 with overweight or obesity · How often: Every 3 years
Condition: Depression · Test: PHQ-2, PHQ-9, Geriatric Depression Scale · Who: All adults · How often: —
Condition: Lung cancer · Test: Low-dose chest CT · Who: Adults 50–80 with a ≥20 pack-year history · How often: Annually
Condition: Breast cancer · Test: Mammogram · Who: Women through age 74 · How often: Per guideline (the manual lists annually; current USPSTF is every 2 years from 40–74)
Condition: Colon cancer · Test: Colonoscopy, gFOBT, FIT, FIT-DNA, flexible sigmoidoscopy, CT colonography · Who: Ages 45–75; after that, a patient-centered decision · How often: Depends on test
Condition: Prostate cancer · Test: PSA · Who: Shared decision, men 55–69 (grade C) · How often: Individualized
Condition: Vision and hearing · Test: — · Who: Not recommended if asymptomatic · How often: —
The most common safety concerns are:
Accidental injuries: falls; burns from fire or scalding
Poisoning: carbon monoxide, medications, cleaning products
Abuse: interpersonal violence; financial and security scams
Falls. About 3 million older adults are treated in EDs for falls each year, and about 20% of falls cause serious injury such as a fracture or TBI.
Three-question fall screen. A "yes" to any question means increased risk.
Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking?
Have you fallen in the past year? If so, how many times, and were you injured?
Gait, strength and balance: Timed Up & Go, 30-Second Chair Stand, 4-Stage Balance Test
Check vitamin D intake and supplement
Look for and optimize comorbidities (e.g., dementia, osteoporosis)
Referrals: eye care, OT home evaluation, podiatry, exercise or PT
Fires and burns. Adults 65 and older are twice as likely to die in a fire.
High-risk situations: stovetop cooking, smoking at home, electrical faults, space heaters, heating pads and electric blankets.
Minor (superficial and partial-thickness) burns can be managed in primary care.
Superficial / partial-thickness burn care: Cool with room-temperature or cool tap water · Refer for: All full-thickness burns
Superficial / partial-thickness burn care: Clean gently with mild soap 2–3 times a day · Refer for: Circumferential extremity burns
Superficial / partial-thickness burn care: Topical agents and dressings 2–3 times a day · Refer for: Inhalation injury
Superficial / partial-thickness burn care: Don't unroof bullae; debride if ruptured · Refer for: Facial burns
Superficial / partial-thickness burn care: Manage pain · Refer for: >10% BSA, severe pain, delayed healing
About 10% of adults 60 and older experience abuse or neglect.
Abuse: physical, sexual, emotional or financial behavior that causes harm, pain, loss or distress.
Neglect: failure to meet an older adult's basic needs.
Offender: unrealistic expectations or negative attitude toward caregiving; dependence on the victim for housing or money.
Victim: inconsistent attitude toward the aggressor; dependence on the aggressor for housing, money or care; self-neglect.
Both: physical or mental health problems, substance use disorder, poor stress coping, chronic relationship problems, previous victimization.
Neglect: malnutrition or starvation, dehydration, lack of medical care, poor hygiene, undermedication.
Abuse: trauma or fractures in unusual areas, patterned injuries, over- or undermedication, inappropriate restraint.
Interventions: ask patients directly. Report confirmed or suspected abuse to Adult Protective Services or police; this is mandatory. Support caregivers.
Pharmacokinetics (how the drug moves through the body)

Property: Absorption · Age-related change: Reduced absorption, GI motility, small-bowel surface area and perfusion; reduced first-pass metabolism · Effect: Altered bioavailability; standard dose may be too little or too much
Property: Distribution · Age-related change: Less lean mass and total body water; lower serum protein · Effect: Altered distribution of water- and fat-soluble drugs; more free (unbound) drug
Property: Metabolism · Age-related change: Reduced hepatic perfusion and CYP450 function · Effect: Slower clearance
Property: Elimination · Age-related change: Reduced renal perfusion, GFR and tubular secretion · Effect: Reduced renal elimination; toxicity
System: CNS · Change: More sensitive to CNS depressants · Effect: Stronger effects from opioids, anesthetics, benzodiazepines and sedatives; more tardive dyskinesia with neuroleptics
System: Autonomic · Change: Less variability and vagal tone · Effect: Orthostatic hypotension; blunted inotropic and chronotropic responses

System: Cardiovascular · Change: Less beta-1 response; vascular stiffness; low-renin state · Effect: Blunted heart-rate response to beta agonists and blockers; higher SBP; ACE inhibitors may be less effective
System: Renal · Change: Kidneys depend more on prostaglandin vasodilation · Effect: NSAIDs cause hyperkalemia and sodium/water retention; TZD-related hyponatremia
Polypharmacy. 22.4% of U.S. adults aged 40–79 take five or more medications. More drugs mean more interactions, adverse effects and errors.
When a new symptom appears, ask whether it's a drug side effect or disease progression.
Don't change several drugs at once.

Beers Criteria (American Geriatrics Society) list potentially inappropriate medications: drugs that raise morbidity or mortality in older adults because of pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic changes. Classes include:
Anticholinergics: first-generation antihistamines, antispasmodics, muscle relaxants
Some anti-infectives and some cardiac agents
Psychiatric drugs: anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, TCAs, some SSRIs and SNRIs

Prescribing cascade (case of Ms. Biggs). A 76-year-old woman takes Advil PM (ibuprofen plus diphenhydramine) for insomnia. She develops dry eyes (anticholinergic effect) and heartburn (NSAID effect). Her PCP adds famotidine and eye drops. The cascade runs:…

Frailty is reduced physiologic, psychologic and/or social function, often with multiple comorbidities and stressors. It raises the risk of hospitalization, residential care, loss of mobility and death.
Fried physical frailty phenotype. A score of ≥3 means frailty.
Unintentional weight loss >10 lb a year (or >5% of body weight)
Slow walking speed (>6–7 seconds to walk 15 feet)
Exercise for mobility, gait, strength and bone density
Referral for comprehensive geriatric assessment, home health, PT/OT

Insomnia is trouble starting, maintaining or consolidating sleep, or poor sleep quality. It must impair cognition, mood, function or energy, and must not be explained by the environment or another disorder (e.g., sleep apnea).
Keep a regular schedule for sleep, exercise and meals.
Avoid stimulants, evening fluids and alcohol.
Use the bed for sleep only.
Get up if still awake after 20 minutes.
First-line in older adults: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I).

Insomnia drug class: Benzodiazepines · Geriatric cautions: Lowest dose, shortest time. Long-term use is linked to dementia. Beers list (falls, cognitive impairment, lethargy, dependence). Schedule IV.

Insomnia drug class: Melatonin receptor agonist (ramelteon) · Geriatric cautions: Best for trouble falling asleep; take only if able to sleep 7–8 hours. No specific geriatric concerns: the safest choice.

Insomnia drug class: Sedative-hypnotics (eszopiclone, zaleplon, zolpidem) · Geriatric cautions: Lowest dose, shortest time. Fewer adverse effects than benzodiazepines, but on the Beers list. Schedule IV.
Insomnia drug class: Trazodone (off-label) · Geriatric cautions: Beers list: anticholinergic effects, sedation, orthostatic hypotension
GFR falls about 50% between ages 50 and 90, with less kidney mass and fewer functional cells.
Renal insufficiency is a pathologic loss of kidney function: eGFR <90, elevated BUN and creatinine, possible proteinuria, abnormal imaging or pathology, and possibly decreased urine output.
Chronic causes: uncontrolled diabetes, hypertension, CVD, rheumatologic disease, others.
Acute causes: dehydration, infection, medication toxicity, ischemia, nephrotoxins.
Treatment: assume it's acute until proven otherwise.
Stop offending drugs: nephrotoxins, renally cleared drugs, and drugs that reduce renal blood flow.
A single abnormal panel (Cr 1.6, BUN 28, eGFR 34) needs more information to judge chronicity.
CKD means eGFR <60 and/or UACR >30 mg/g for more than 3 months. Creatinine comes from muscle, and muscle mass falls with age, which can make creatinine misleading.
CKD management. At every stage: control underlying disease, reduce CVD risk, cut sodium, prevent AKI, and keep healthy habits and weight.
Stage: 1 · GFR: >90 · Interventions: Reduce sodium; healthy habits and weight
Stage: 2 · GFR: 60–89 · Interventions: Same as stage 1
Stage: 3a · GFR: 45–59 · Interventions: Review medications; consider nephrology referral
Stage: 3b · GFR: 30–44 · Interventions: Review medications; diagnose and treat anemia
Stage: 4 · GFR: 15–29 · Interventions: Review medications; lower protein intake; treat anemia; prepare for dialysis
Depression is common in older adults and adds to disability, medication use, hospitalization and poor quality of life.
First step: determine whether the patient meets DSM-5 criteria before diagnosing or treating.

Assess for: suicidality; psychosis and mania; contributing drugs (benzodiazepines, alcohol, opioids); medical conditions (thyroid disease, diabetes, chronic pain, malnutrition); personal and family history of depression.
Expected SSRI effects in older adults: hyponatremia (SIADH), anorexia, parkinsonism/extrapyramidal effects, bleeding, falls. Sinus tachycardia is not expected; SSRIs tend to cause bradycardia.

Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of SBP ≥20 or DBP ≥10 mmHg on standing. It can cause lightheadedness, syncope or angina with position changes. Example: Mrs. Dalton, 69, with heart failure, just started furosemide and has fallen twice getting out of bed.…
Patient lies down for 5 minutes; measure BP and pulse.
Patient stands for 1 minute; measure again.
Patient stands 2 more minutes; measure again.
Medications: antihypertensives, vasodilators, nitrates, TCAs, opioids
Medical disorders: neurodegenerative disease, diabetic neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction
Avoid triggers: alcohol, large meals, heat, high-intensity exercise.
Use physical maneuvers such as leg crossing and squatting.
About 40% of ambulatory older adults have chronic pain, usually in the hips, back or knees. The goals are to reduce pain intensity and improve function.
Nonpharmacologic interventions. Continue them even after adding drugs.
Oral NSAIDs, if there are no contraindications.
NSAID contraindications include uncontrolled HTN, heart failure, reduced GFR, alcohol use disorder and prior stroke. A patient on bisphosphonates for osteoporosis can be a reasonable NSAID candidate.

Who · Palliative care: Any patient with a chronic, progressive disease, regardless of stage, treatment or age (e.g., COPD with breathlessness and anxiety) · Hospice: Terminal illness with life expectancy <6 months
Focus · Palliative care: Quality of life and symptom management; curative treatment can continue · Hospice: Comfort and quality of life at end of life
Payment and setting · Palliative care: Varies · Hospice: Medicare and some private insurers; available in most settings, including nursing facilities
Competence is a legal term for global decision-making ability.
It is presumed until proven otherwise.
It isn't determined by diagnosis or status, and it isn't judged by outcome. Competent people make bad decisions all the time.
It is task-specific, and state laws vary.
Capacity is a medical term for the ability to make decisions about care. It has four components:

The provider's role: check for communication barriers, assess the four components, and use formal tools (Aid to Capacity Evaluation, Hopkins Competency Assessment Test). Do cognitive testing if it helps the decision.
If family question a patient's decision-making, assess the patient to see whether the concerns are valid.
Living will: a legal document describing how a person wants to be treated if dying or permanently unable to decide.
Durable power of attorney for health care: names the decision-maker.

Erikson stage 8: integrity vs. despair (age >65 to end of life). The person reflects on life with wisdom and fulfillment, or with regret and despair (e.g., "Did I have a meaningful life?"), shaped by past experiences, relationships and meaning.

FNP: Preconception care; pregnancy diagnosis; prenatal care up to the third trimester; primary care problems during pregnancy and postpartum · AGNP: Preconception care; pregnancy diagnosis; referral for prenatal care; primary care problems during pregnancy…

FNP: FNP exam: about 3% of questions (4–6) on pregnancy · AGNP: AGNP exam: a pregnancy-specific question is unlikely, but a primary care question about a patient who is or could be pregnant is possible
The purpose is to find and reduce risks to fertility or a healthy pregnancy, and to prevent unplanned pregnancy. Routinely ask women of childbearing age about plans for conception or contraception.
Avoid medications and substances that are unsafe in pregnancy. For example, stop ACE inhibitors such as enalapril.
Folic acid 400 mcg daily for average risk.
Consider the partner's health and genetic risks.
Update immunizations. MMR must be given ≥1 month before conception.
Assess the patient's neural tube defect (NTD) risk.
The neural tube develops 26–28 days after conception, often before a pregnancy is recognized.
Average risk: 400 mcg (0.4 mg) daily, starting at least 1 month before conception.
High risk: 1,000–4,000 mcg/day for 1–3 months before conception and through the first trimester, then 400 mcg until 6 weeks postpartum. Doses over 1,000 mcg/day should be managed by an obstetrician.
Either parent, or a first-degree relative, with an NTD. A second- or third-degree relative raises risk mildly.
Maternal drugs that reduce folate availability: triamterene, trimethoprim, sulfasalazine.
Maternal conditions that reduce absorption or increase clearance: gastric bypass, IBD.
NTDs include spina bifida, anencephaly and encephalocele. Cleft palate is not an NTD.
Symptoms: amenorrhea, nausea, breast changes, fatigue, constipation, food aversions or cravings, mood changes, urinary frequency.
Exam signs (present in the first 4–8 weeks)
Goodell sign: softening of the cervix
Chadwick sign: bluish discoloration of the cervix
Hegar sign: compressibility of the cervical isthmus on bimanual exam
Normal physiologic findings include nasal congestion, mild exertional dyspnea and a soft systolic murmur. Increased BP is not expected. BP normally falls in early pregnancy.
Urine hCG: Sensitive 9–12 days after conception · Serum hCG: Sensitive 8–11 days after conception

Urine hCG: Sensitivity varies widely; expensive home tests may beat cheap office tests · Serum hCG: Qualitative: rarely needed unless a false negative is suspected. Quantitative: should rise predictably in the first trimester.
Estimated due date (EDD) guides the timing of prenatal care, birth interventions and growth monitoring.
Naegele rule: LMP − 3 months + 7 days, plus 1 year.
Gold standard: first-trimester ultrasound, which establishes gestational age.
Diabetes found early in pregnancy. Diagnostic criteria are the same as for nonpregnant adults: fasting glucose, random glucose or A1c. The 3-hour GTT is not used to diagnose preexisting diabetes.
Nausea and vomiting. It is pregnancy-related when it starts around 5–6 weeks and resolves by about 12 weeks. Onset after 10 weeks, fever or bilious vomiting suggest another cause.
Nonpharmacologic: ginger, ginger ale, saltines; small cold snacks every 1–2 hours; avoid triggers (smells, hot foods) and low blood sugar.
First-line drugs: pyridoxine (vitamin B6) or doxylamine plus pyridoxine (Diclegis).
Constipation. The safest treatment is a bulk-forming agent such as psyllium (Metamucil). Avoid mineral oil and castor oil.
Avoid fetal drug exposure when possible, especially in the first trimester.
Weigh risks and benefits. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and refer to OB/GYN if safety is unclear.
Patients should call before starting or stopping any medication.
Pregnancy categories: OTC drugs still use A–X. Prescription categories were eliminated.
2015 FDA Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) sections: pregnancy exposure registry, risk summary, data, clinical considerations.
Safety tier: Safe · Examples: Folic acid, B6, levothyroxine, many vaccines
Safety tier: Probably safe (some safety data) · Examples: Penicillins, cephalosporins, prednisone, insulin, sertraline, triptans, nifedipine; inhaled budesonide (continue asthma controller)

Asthma. Continue inhaled budesonide at the same dose. Uncontrolled asthma is a greater risk to the fetus.
Acute cystitis in pregnancy. Treat empirically and adjust to the culture. Fosfomycin is effective and a good choice in the first trimester. Get a test-of-cure culture after treatment.

Cramping is usually normal, from hormones or the growing uterus. Cramping that worsens or comes with bleeding suggests ectopic pregnancy or threatened abortion; most first-trimester ectopics end in miscarriage. Fetal viability is at more than 22–26 weeks.
Maternal weight affects neonatal morbidity and mortality and the child's later risk of diabetes, hypertension and cerebrovascular disease.
Exercise. Continuing an established activity such as running is safe. Avoid contact sports (boxing), fall-risk activities (horseback riding) and overheating (hot yoga).

Screen all pregnant patients for alcohol, tobacco, opioids, methamphetamine and cocaine. No level is safe; these substances are teratogenic at every stage. Counseling is effective. About 1 in 7 pregnant patients report alcohol use and 1 in 20 report binge…
Substance: Opioids · Complications: Placental abruption, fetal demise, growth restriction, preeclampsia, preterm labor, miscarriage, postpartum hemorrhage
Substance: Marijuana · Complications: Abnormal brain development (ADD, behavior problems), growth restriction
Substance: Alcohol · Complications: Stillbirth, miscarriage, fetal alcohol syndrome and fetal alcohol effects
Substance: Smoking · Complications: Stillbirth, PPROM, low birth weight, placental abruption, doubled preterm-birth risk, sudden unexpected infant death
Opioid use disorder: medication for OUD, including buprenorphine, can be started in pregnancy.
Toxoplasmosis: don't clean the cat box; wear gloves when gardening; avoid undercooked or cured meats, soil and unwashed produce.
Others: parvovirus B19 (fifth disease), COVID-19, Zika, influenza, Listeria, CMV, varicella.

Avoid live vaccines: MMR and varicella.

Quantitative hCG fails to double every 24–72 hours.

Cause unknown. Often asymptomatic and found on the 18–20 week ultrasound.

Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) is membrane rupture before contractions begin, at <37 weeks.
Gold standard: pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior vaginal vault on speculum exam.
Ultrasound: amniotic fluid normal to low-normal.
Other tests: PAMG-1 assay; nitrazine pH; fern test; dye instillation (tampon test). ROM Plus (PP12 + AFP) is no longer recommended.

New hypertension: BP ≥140/90 on two occasions
Delivery (by 40 weeks or earlier) is the definitive treatment.
Rest in the left lateral position to take pressure off the vena cava.
Balanced diet with moderate protein and sodium.
Hospitalize if BP stays ≥160/110 despite bed rest.
Postpartum blues resolve by about 2 weeks.
Postpartum depression uses the same DSM-5-TR criteria as major depression, with peripartum onset.
Example: at 4 weeks postpartum, a positive PHQ-9 with anhedonia means postpartum depression.

Typical features: anhedonia, lack of interest in the infant, anxiety about caring for the infant, a negative view of the infant's temperament. An increasing need for support and reassurance is less characteristic.
Screen with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale: 10 items, under 5 minutes, easy to score, in 50+ languages.
Consequences: problems with breastfeeding and bonding, harm to child health and development, suicide.
Treatment: psychotherapy, then SSRIs. Sertraline and escitalopram are the safest.
Components: risk assessment, health promotion, education and therapeutic intervention. The goal is to prevent, or promptly recognize and treat, maternal and fetal complications.
First: confirm the due date and fetal development; identify abnormalities.
Second: confirm dates and size; identify abnormalities and bleeding.
Third: confirm size; identify complications, bleeding and fetal position (e.g., breech).

Fundal height (McDonald rule). Measure in cm from the symphysis pubis to the top of the uterus. From 18–34 weeks, fundal height in cm ≈ gestational age in weeks. Refer if it differs by more than 2 cm.
Screens for: Down syndrome, trisomy 18 and NTDs.

Management: insulin (NPH, aspart, lispro have safety data). Metformin is an ACOG option (not ADA) and is safe throughout pregnancy.
Rh(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM). Rh incompatibility occurs when the mother is Rh-negative and the fetus Rh-positive. Screen at the first visit of every pregnancy.
Rh-negative with a positive anti-D antibody screen: don't give RhoGAM. It doesn't work once alloimmunization has occurred.
Rh-negative with a negative anti-D screen: give RhoGAM:
after delivery of an Rh-positive newborn
after any event with fetomaternal bleeding (trauma, bleeding, miscarriage, abortion), even if antibody status is unknown
28–36 weeks: fundal height for growth restriction; fetal heart tones and activity; Tdap and RSV; STIs if high risk.
36–41 weeks: fetal presentation (cephalic or not); GBS screen; accelerated growth.
Macrosomia: >4,500 g with diabetes, >5,000 g without.
Routine cervical cancer screening is avoided; cervical checks for dilation and effacement increase.
Kick counts (from 28 weeks). The patient lies on her left side 30 minutes after eating and counts movements. A healthy fetus moves 3–5 times in 1 hour; most move much more.
Screen at 35–37 weeks with vaginal and rectal swabs.

Complications: pregnancy loss, preterm delivery, stillbirth.

Use the free CDC Vaccine Schedules app. Don't memorize the schedule; on the exam, make the safe clinical decision.
Live attenuated vaccines are weakened live viruses that must replicate to produce immunity, so they can cause a viral-replication reaction (fever, rash).
Examples: MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza, rotavirus, smallpox, yellow fever.
Never give to pregnant or immunocompromised patients.
Give live vaccines on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart; otherwise efficacy drops.
Monitor for 15 minutes after vaccination, because of the risk of syncope.
Spacing. Doses given up to 4 days early are valid. Doses given 5 or more days early are invalid and must be repeated.
Unknown vaccine history. Vaccinate as if the child has never been vaccinated, or draw titers for antibodies to vaccine-preventable illness. Both approaches are acceptable.
Take time to listen; solicit and welcome questions.
Don't dismiss the family from the practice. Schedule the child and defer the vaccine discussion until a therapeutic relationship is established.
Have them call ahead before bringing an ill child.
Alert other providers that the child is unimmunized.
Have the caregiver sign the CDC refusal-to-vaccinate form.
Exam tips: establish a connection, speak softly, go slowly, let the child touch the equipment, have the parent hold the child gently, and save the ear exam and anything frightening for last.
Acute otitis media (AOM) is infection of the middle ear.
Bacterial: S. pneumoniae (40–50%), H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
AOM: cloudy, bulging TM with impaired mobility. OME: noninfectious fluid.
A red TM alone, without bulging or immobility, just means inflammation. Crying causes it too.
Antibiotics: AOM with otorrhea · Observation, with follow-up in 48–72 h: AOM without otorrhea, age ≥2 years
Antibiotics: AOM with severe symptoms: toxic-appearing, pain >48 h, temperature ≥102.2°F · Observation, with follow-up in 48–72 h: Unilateral AOM without otorrhea
Bilateral AOM without otorrhea, 6 months to 2 years
AOM situation: Initial choice · Antibiotic: Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day
AOM situation: Antibiotic in the past 30 days · Antibiotic: Amoxicillin/clavulanate
AOM situation: Mild or questionable penicillin reaction · Antibiotic: Cefdinir, cefpodoxime, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone
AOM situation: Severe penicillin allergy · Antibiotic: Azithromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin
Refer for recurrent AOM: ≥3 well-documented episodes in 6 months, or 4 in 12 months, despite appropriate antibiotics.
Strawberry tongue (raised red papillae) in an ill child is most often from strep pharyngitis (scarlet fever).
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) usually begins before age 2.
Suspect it with: delayed language or communication milestones; regression in social or language skills; an affected sibling; developmental concerns raised by caregivers.
Screen at the 9-, 18-, 24- and 30-month visits, and whenever concerns arise. Use the M-CHAT-R/F (18–30 months), and have a referral source ready.
Bullying risk factors: low self-esteem, being perceived as different or weak, few friends, depression or anxiety.

Eating disorders: children with eating disorders often have comorbid psychiatric conditions. Boys and children of every socioeconomic status are affected, and many patients are not underweight at diagnosis.

Common: more than 90% of school-age children. Most are migraine, tension, cluster or chronic daily headache. Secondary headaches are uncommon. Benign causes include viral illness, stress and eye strain.
History: pattern, burden, family and past history, medications.
Exam: head circumference, growth trajectory, EENT, full neuro exam.
Imaging: MRI preferred (CT if something is developing rapidly) for red flags, an abnormal exam, or underlying disease such as sickle cell or immunodeficiency.
Headache red flags (worry about an intracranial process)
Headache that wakes the child, or other signs of raised ICP
Neurologic findings: persistent vomiting, altered mental status, ataxia
Recurrent localized headache or a chronic progressive pattern
Migraine is the most common acute recurrent headache in children. Diagnose by ICHD-3 criteria. It often comes with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and auras are common.
Nonpharmacologic: eliminate triggers, reduce stress, rest.
Prophylactic: cyproheptadine syrup for young children; vitamin B2, melatonin and magnesium are safe and well tolerated.

Acute symptomatic (provoked) seizure: caused by an acute state such as hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, fever (febrile seizure), toxins, or intracranial inflammation (bleeding, meningitis). It is not epilepsy; treat the cause.
Unprovoked seizure: no provoking condition, or a preexisting brain lesion or progressive neurologic disorder.
Epilepsy: an enduring predisposition to seizures. Either two unprovoked seizures >24 h apart, or one unprovoked seizure with high recurrence risk.
History to take: time and setting; what the child was doing; new medications; systemic symptoms; aura; first sign; duration; loss of alertness; bowel or bladder loss; postictal phase and its length.
A focal seizure with no cause found: order an MRI and refer to neurology.
Lead toxicity masquerades as iron-deficiency anemia.
Sources: old house paint dust, water, food, lead pipes, mouthing toys or jewelry.
Symptoms: fatigue, GI upset (stomachache, constipation), irritability, renal changes.
Cognitive and behavioral damage is irreversible.
Young children are more susceptible because of an incomplete blood–brain barrier.
Peaks: term infants at days 3–4; preterm at days 5–7, with greater toxicity risk.
Treatment thresholds come from risk charts: bilirubin level vs. age in hours. Escalation of care is based on the bilirubin level.
Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic.
Increased production (hemolysis): ABO incompatibility, sepsis, G6PD deficiency, macrosomic infants.
Decreased removal: enzyme defects such as Crigler–Najjar and Gilbert syndromes; maternal or fetal endocrine problems.
Increased enterohepatic circulation: inadequate feeding, breastfeeding, intestinal obstruction.
Asymptomatic: use a risk calculator (gestational age, postnatal age, stability). Phototherapy is first-line.

Symptomatic: total bilirubin >25–32 mg/dL. Free bilirubin crosses the blood–brain barrier and causes irreversible bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction (BIND). Escalate care and consider exchange transfusion.
Mental status: sleepy but arousable, poor feeding, poor suck, irritability
Cry: high-pitched or shrill, hard to console, weak or absent
X-linked loss of a protective red cell enzyme. It can cause hemolysis or stay silent for life.
Screen newborns with severe jaundice and anyone with a family history.
Prevalence: Kurdish Jewish 70%, Sardinian 4–35%, Nigerian 22%, Thai 17%, African American 12%.
Acute hemolysis is triggered by oxidative stress:
Sickle cell disease (SCD). Sickled RBCs carry oxygen poorly and clump, causing hemolytic anemia and vaso-occlusion: acute and chronic pain and tissue ischemia in every organ system.
Functional asplenia makes these children highly susceptible to infection, which can trigger a crisis. Fever can be life-threatening.
Give prophylactic penicillin BID; continue it at well visits.
Live vaccines are NOT contraindicated in SCD. Keep up all immunizations.
Leukemia is cancer of the bone marrow, producing abnormal RBCs, WBCs and/or platelets. It is the most common childhood cancer.
Symptoms: anorexia, weight loss, fever, hepatosplenomegaly (>60%), bleeding (50%), persistent bone pain in the long bones (21–38%), lymphadenopathy (50%).
Concerning lymph nodes: enlarged, nontender, firm, rubbery or matted, fixed.
CBC with differential: thrombocytopenia in 85%; WBC normal or high, with blasts; anemia.
Peripheral smear: myeloid or lymphoid blasts.
Pancytopenia (low WBC, RBC and platelets) means bone marrow failure: think leukemia.
Children's airways are tiny, so constriction or obstruction causes big problems.
Viruses are the most common cause in children <5. RSV now has prevention products.
If bacterial: S. pneumoniae (drug-resistant strains common). Over age 5: S. pneumoniae, then M. pneumoniae.
The most sensitive sign in infants is increased respiratory rate.
Chest X-ray: infiltrates. It may be normal early, especially with dehydration. No follow-up film is needed if the child improves.
CBC: bacterial infection shows more segs and bands, WBC >15,000.
Tip: When the poly and lymph percentages are far apart, the infection is likely bacterial.
First-line: high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day in divided doses.
Recent antibiotics: amoxicillin/clavulanate or a third-generation cephalosporin.
Avoid doxycycline under age 8 and fluoroquinolones under 18.
Never exceed the adult maximum. For an 11-year-old calculated at 3,680 mg/day, give 1,000 mg TID.
Supportive care: fluids, antipyretics, rest. Hospitalize and give oxygen for respiratory distress.
Vaccine: PCV 15/20: 4 doses by 18 months. High-risk children >2 years: PCV plus PPSV23 · Protects against: Strep pneumoniae
Vaccine: DTaP (age <7) · Protects against: Pertussis (whooping cough)
Vaccine: Hib · Protects against: H. influenzae type b: pneumonia, meningitis, epiglottitis
Vaccine: RSV · Protects against: Monoclonal antibody for infants <8 months, and 8–19 months with risk factors; maternal vaccine at 32–36 weeks; adults ≥75, or 60–74 with risk factors

PPSV23 indications include diabetes, chronic heart or lung disease (asthma counts only if treated with high-dose oral steroids), immunocompromise (e.g., leukemia), cochlear implants and CSF leaks. Mild persistent asthma alone is not an indication.
Children <8 years getting their first doses need 2 doses 4 weeks apart.
Egg allergy of any severity: give the routine flu vaccine. No special precautions and no screening are needed.
Bronchiolitis is a self-limited lower respiratory infection, mostly in children <2 years (RSV most common). The diagnosis is clinical.
Course: URI for 1–3 days, wheezing peaks on days 3–5, resolution over 2–4 weeks.
Signs: fever (lower with RSV, higher with adenovirus); cough; thick nasal secretions; respiratory distress if severe.
Management is supportive: education, nasal suction, monitoring for dehydration. No bronchodilators and no steroids.
Admit for respiratory distress (nasal flaring, retractions) or poor intake, for fluids, suctioning and oxygen.
Viral; most common at 6 months to 3 years.
Signs: fever, inspiratory stridor, barking cough, hoarseness, worse at night.
Steeple sign on AP neck X-ray.
Mild croup: give a single dose of oral dexamethasone.
Asthma is the most common chronic childhood illness and a frequent cause of missed school.
History: symptom patterns; triggers (animals, smoke, perfume, seasons, medications); personal or family history of atopy.
Suspect asthma under age 5 with recurrent wheezing (one episode plus symptoms between episodes, or two in 12 months), no likely alternative cause, and improvement with SABA, with or without ICS.
A personal or family history of allergic disease strengthens the diagnosis. Wheezing before age 1 is more likely bronchiolitis.
MART with ICS/formoterol is not routine under age 5.

Step, ages <5: 2: Mild persistent · NAEPP: Low-dose ICS daily + SABA prn · GINA: Low-dose ICS daily + SABA prn; consider referral
Step, ages <5: 3: Moderate · NAEPP: Medium-dose ICS daily + SABA prn; refer · GINA: ICS daily + SABA prn, or ICS + LTRA; consider referral
Step, ages <5: 4: Severe · NAEPP: Medium-dose ICS-LABA + SABA prn · GINA: Continue controller and refer
Step, ages 5–11 (NAEPP) / 6–11 (GINA): 1 · NAEPP: SABA prn · GINA: SABA + ICS prn
Step, ages 5–11 (NAEPP) / 6–11 (GINA): 2 · NAEPP: Low-dose ICS daily + SABA prn · GINA: Low-dose ICS daily

Consider referral at step 3; refer at step 4.
ICS and growth: inhaled corticosteroids rarely inhibit growth (at most about 1 cm).
Viral-triggered wheeze in a known asthmatic that improves with a nebulizer: prescribe a 5-day oral steroid burst.
Newborn screening in all 50 states; confirm with a sweat chloride test.
Faulty CFTR channels don't export chloride, causing excess salt loss in sweat and thick mucus.
Multisystem: GI tract, lungs, reproductive tract, sweat glands.
frequent sinus and lower respiratory infections
pancreatic duct blockage, causing weight loss, greasy stools and dysmotility
Normal heart rate: birth 120–160; age 3, 80–120; age 6, 70–110.
Femoral pulses should be strong and equal to brachial pulses. Weak or delayed femoral pulses suggest coarctation of the aorta.
BP depends on age, sex and height, and rises with BMI.
Start screening at age 3, then annually. Measure at every visit if risk factors are present.
Hypertension: BP ≥95th percentile (or ≥130/80) on 3 separate visits.

Congenital heart disease. Murmurs are common: about 1% of children have CHD and 10% of those are significant. CHD may be found at birth or at 6 weeks or later. "Murmurs are judged by the company they keep."

Intussusception is telescoping of the bowel into itself, causing inflammation and obstruction.

Loretta Ford, EdD, PNP, FAAN, founded the first NP program in 1965 with Dr. Henry Silver, MD, at the University of Colorado. It was a pediatric program, created because physicians were leaving primary care for specialties.
The role met resistance from nurses (over the title) and from other professionals (over practice without physician supervision).
More than 400 NP programs and more than 385,000 licensed NPs.
Prescriptive authority in all 50 states and DC.

Population focus: FNP 70.3%; AGPC 8.9%; PMHNP 6.5%; AGAC 6.1%; peds primary care 2.4%; women's health 2.2%; peds acute care 0.6%; neonatal 0.5%. Retired exams: adult PC 5.7%, adult AC 2.9%, gerontology 0.9%.
Settings: 48% physician offices, 22% hospitals, 9% outpatient centers, 4% other practitioner offices.
Bureau of Labor Statistics: NP jobs projected to grow 45% from 2022 to 2032 (118,600 new jobs).
The four APRN roles: NP, CNM, CRNA and CNS. All require a BSN and graduate education. The CNS needs no license beyond the RN in some states.
APRN Consensus Model (2008, with NCSBN) defines an APRN as someone who:
completed an accredited graduate program in one of the four roles
passed a national certification exam measuring role and population competencies, and maintains continued competence
has advanced clinical knowledge and skill for direct and indirect care
builds on RN competencies with greater depth, synthesis, complexity and autonomy
is responsible and accountable for health promotion and maintenance: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation (including prescribing) and evaluation
has clinical experience sufficient for the intended license
is licensed in one of the four roles

Common APRN responsibilities: assessment and diagnosis; treatment planning; direct care; health promotion and disease prevention; research and QI; collaboration; leadership; education; advocacy and policy.
Advanced competencies for complex practice, faculty and leadership roles.
Better patient outcomes and stronger leadership.
Credits and time that better match the credential.
A practice doctorate for those who don't want a research focus.
Attracts people from non-nursing backgrounds and increases practice faculty.
Relationship building and the human experience

AACN Essentials (2021) set core competencies for entry-level and advanced nursing education: identical competencies with level-specific sub-competencies. They span four spheres of care: disease prevention and health promotion, chronic disease care,…
Competency-based education (CBE), as AACN defines it, is instruction, assessment, feedback, self-reflection and reporting based on students demonstrating the expected knowledge, attitudes and skills.
The adult learner is responsible for mastery and works with clear performance expectations.
The learner reflects, analyzes, judges, resolves, discovers, interacts and creates, and keeps self-reflecting in practice.

NONPF core competencies: leadership; quality; practice inquiry; technology and information literacy; policy; health delivery systems; ethics; independent practice. Plus population-focused competencies.
Scope of practice is the set of services a qualified professional is competent and permitted to perform under their license.
Education, training and certification: role and population, national certification, additional training (e.g., joint injections, Nexplanon).
The state Nurse Practice Act, as interpreted by the Board of Nursing.
Am I within my scope? Ask four questions:
Am I educated (role and population) to do it?
Is it restricted by state law or the BON?
Am I competent and comfortable doing it?
Accreditation: a recognized agency approves the education program or certification.
Certification recognizes knowledge, skills and achievement of professional standards.
Education: formal graduate or postgraduate certificate preparation.
State practice environment: full, reduced or restricted. The BON sets rules on controlled substances, off-label use, weight-loss drugs and CE.
State Board of Pharmacy: compounding, the PDMP, controlled-substance limits.
Medicare requires an NPI and permits direct billing. Services must be medically necessary and within scope.
Medicare credentialing requires certification and state licensure.
Scope vs. standards: scope defines the boundaries; standards describe the expected level of care.
Standards of practice keep practice safe and competent:
Emphasize priorities: education, shared decision-making, optimal health, continual competence.
Assure quality and continued competence: QA, record review, current EBP, certification, legal compliance.
Fill integral roles: mentor, preceptor, educator, researcher, advocate.
Use research as the basis for practice.
Assessment: comprehensive history; age-appropriate exam; preventive and diagnostic tests; risk factors; social determinants of health.
Diagnosis: diagnostic reasoning; synthesize data; a prioritized differential.
Plan: tests; priorities for patient, family and community; drug and non-drug orders; education tailored to health literacy; consults and referrals by evidence and shared decision-making.
Evaluation: is the plan working? Document outcomes; reassess and modify with the patient and family.
CC in the patient's own words
HPI: onset, duration, severity, location, modifying factors
FH: parents, siblings, children, with ages and causes of death
SH: environment, behaviors, marital status, education, diet, smoking
Exam: general appearance, head to toe
Differential, ranked by probability, and the working diagnosis
Management of each problem, with rationale, therapeutics and education
Evaluation: follow-up, expected course, referral, complications
Consultation: asking for advice on a diagnosis or plan; you keep the patient.
Referral: another provider takes over ongoing treatment of a specific problem.
When to use them: you need advice, the treatment failed, a specialized procedure is needed, the patient asks, or it is beyond your scope.
Interprofessional collaboration (from The Future of Nursing 2020–2030, NASEM 2021) has four core competencies:
Values and ethics: respect and trust, toward equitable care.
Roles and responsibilities: know and explain your role and understand others'.
Teams and teamwork: effective leadership, better outcomes, fewer errors.
Evidence-based practice (EBP) applies research findings to daily care and decisions.
Ask a clinical question, using PICO-T: patient or population, intervention, comparison, outcome, time.
Obtain the best literature: search databases with key words and select articles.
Integrate the evidence with clinical expertise and patient preferences and values.

Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are systematically developed, evidence-informed recommendations that weigh risks and benefits. They are not fixed rules. They combine traditional standards of care with research.
Construction by a small, representative group.
Testing by professionals not involved in development, for clarity, consistency and acceptability.
Reproducible (another group would reach the same recommendations)
Reliable (another clinician would apply them the same way)
Guidelines must also be disseminated (journals, targeted mailings, education) and implemented, addressing barriers such as time, cost and staff. Developers should disclose conflicts of interest.
Disagreements between guidelines are usually minor (e.g., screening start age). They come from weak evidence, small samples or differing resources.
Pluralism: the U.S. has many guideline makers, including specialty societies, private groups, AHRQ and USPSTF. The U.K. has a single body, NICE.

The standard of care is the level of care relevant to a specific situation. It decides liability: would a similarly credentialed and experienced provider with the same resources have acted the same way?
To prove negligence (breach), the plaintiff must show all four:
Duty: the provider owed a duty of care.
Causation: the negligence caused or contributed to the harm.
Prescription errors (wrong drug, dose or condition)
Intentional harm, which may also be criminal
A breach can occur through error, omission, delay, or inappropriate use of resources.
Typical limits: •1 million per claim, •3 million aggregate.
Claims-made policies need tail coverage after you leave (or "nose" coverage purchased by a new insurer).
Occurrence policies cover any incident during the policy period, whenever it is filed.
Coverage pays for the defense attorney, lost wages, court costs and board representation.
Employer policies may have low limits, may not cover outside or volunteer work or board hearings, and may not cover suits filed after you leave.
Created by: Title IV of the Health Care Quality Improvement Act of 1986, with later additions in 1987 and in HIPAA 1996. It is run by HHS/HRSA.
Purpose: improve quality, protect the public, fight fraud and abuse, and stop incompetent providers moving between states.
adverse license, privilege and professional society actions
reports from law enforcement, peer review and health plans
attorneys, only with proof a hospital failed to query
Self-query: keep your address current; you can dispute a report or submit a statement.
Rank: 1 · Design: Systematic review / meta-analysis · Description: Combines many studies. A meta-analysis is level 1 only when paired with a systematic review.
Rank: 2 · Design: Randomized controlled trial · Description: Random assignment to control or intervention; controls other factors
Rank: 3 · Design: Cohort · Description: Groups with different exposures followed forward for outcomes
Rank: 4 · Design: Case-control · Description: Cases matched to controls; looks back (retrospective)
Rank: 5 · Design: Cross-sectional · Description: One point in time; surveys
Rank: 6 · Design: Case report or series · Description: A single patient or a small series
Rank: 7 · Design: Expert opinion · Description: Consensus
Rank: 8 · Design: Anecdotal · Description: Clinical observations
Data · Quantitative: Numbers, testing a predefined hypothesis · Qualitative: Words, pictures or objects, exploring and describing
Designs · Quantitative: Experimental, observational · Qualitative: Phenomenologic, ethnographic, grounded theory, historical, case study, action research
Researcher · Quantitative: Objective; controls conditions · Qualitative: Interprets the data as it emerges; subjectivity accepted
Phenomenology: lived experience, through participants' descriptions.
Ethnography: cultural groups in their natural setting.
Grounded theory: constant comparison of data to develop a theory (e.g., why patients miss follow-ups).
Historical: historical data checked for authenticity (external) and accuracy (internal) (e.g., Pearl Harbor).
Action research: investigation plus intervention to solve a problem (e.g., a teacher testing a new reading method).
Applicability is how far results apply to your setting and patient.
Report key characteristics: efficacy vs. effectiveness.
Summarize applicability across the body of evidence.
Population: do my patients match the study's age, ethnicity, SES and problem?
Intervention: how does it compare with routine practice?
Comparison: is the comparator the best alternative?
Outcome: are the most important benefits and harms measured, over a relevant time?
S stands for setting or study type; T for time frame.
GRADE rates the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations transparently.
Level: A · Quality: High · Meaning: More research is very unlikely to change confidence. Several high-quality, consistent studies.
Level: B · Quality: Moderate · Meaning: More research may change the estimate. One high-quality study, or several with limitations.
Level: C · Quality: Low · Meaning: More research is likely to change the estimate. Studies with severe limitations.
Level: D · Quality: Very low · Meaning: Any estimate is very uncertain. Expert opinion or no direct evidence.
High: the true effect is similar to the estimate.

Certainty goes down with: risk of bias, imprecision, inconsistency, indirectness, publication bias. Certainty goes up with: a very large effect, a dose–response gradient, or residual confounding that would shrink the effect.
Framework: Consequentialism (utilitarian) · Idea: Judge actions only by their consequences · Advantage: Promotes happiness and utility · Disadvantage: Ignores justice for minorities
Framework: Deontology (duty-based) · Idea: Follow the rules, regardless of consequences · Advantage: Respects duty and persons · Disadvantage: Underweights happiness and social utility

Framework: Principlism · Idea: Use the four principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) plus virtue and practical wisdom · Advantage: A common moral language · Disadvantage: No method for choosing between principles
Beneficence: act in the patient's best interest.
Autonomy: the patient lives by their own reasons and choices.
Nonmaleficence: do no harm; the patient is no worse off after care.
Justice: distributive justice, with fair and equitable treatment for all.
Fiduciary relationship: the provider acts in the patient's best interest (trust).
Fidelity: keep promises; give competent, safe care.
Paternalism: deciding for a patient without their explicit consent, believing it is in their interest.
A patient may refuse beneficial treatment (autonomy).
A provider may decline to give a treatment they believe does more harm than good (nonmaleficence). This is situational and regulated by the state.
Informed consent is essential to autonomy, for treatment or research. Discuss and document:
the risks and benefits of the alternatives
Also document the patient's participation, avoid coercion, and give your recommendation and reasoning.
Subjective: what does this patient need to know?
Reasonable patient: what would an average patient need to know? This is the most commonly used standard.
Reasonable provider: what would a typical provider disclose?
Incapacity. Proof may be needed. Without a designated decision-maker, follow the state hierarchy of surrogates; if that fails, a court appoints a guardian.
Life-threatening emergency with no time to get consent.

Minors (unemancipated) can't consent; get informed permission from a parent or guardian. Emancipated minors include those who are married, in the military, financially independent, or parents themselves. Check state law.
Research ethics. IRBs were established by the National Research Act of 1974, after the Tuskegee syphilis study.
Valid research consent requires disclosure, competency and voluntariness.
Consent can be waived for minimal-risk studies (e.g., retrospective chart reviews).
Shared decision-making (SDM) is a form of informed consent, used when more than one reasonable option exists. It helps reduce disparities.
unbiased evidence on the options, including no intervention
clinician skill in communicating and tailoring that evidence
the patient's goals, preferences and concerns, including treatment burden
Privacy Act: 12 exceptions to written consent for disclosure
Need to know within the agency (the most litigated)
Health or safety of an individual

EMTALA (42 U.S.C. §1395dd, part of COBRA) comes from beneficence and justice. Hospitals must screen and stabilize emergency patients regardless of ability to pay. Problems arise in deciding what counts as an emergency and when a patient is stable.
Confidentiality and HIPAA. Confidentiality comes from the fiduciary relationship and from autonomy: the patient controls who knows their health status.
Exceptions: imminent danger to the patient or others; certain infectious diseases; reportable STIs.
Continuity of care: the patient may choose future providers and accept or refuse referrals.
The right to elevate unaddressed concerns (42 CFR §482.13, 1986).
Coverage of preexisting conditions without extra charges
No lifetime or annual dollar limits on essential benefits
You can't lose coverage for getting sick
New benefits such as mental health coverage
Health informatics: acquiring, storing, retrieving and using health data.
Health IT: scheduling and billing, EHRs, personal health records, e-prescribing, health apps.
42 CFR Part 2: extra privacy for substance use treatment records.
HITECH Act (2009, part of ARRA): promoted EHR adoption and meaningful use.
HIPAA (1996): privacy of medical information, especially in employment.
FDASIA (2012): faster access to digital records; drug and device safety.
21st Century Cures Act (2016): speeds medical technology and patient access.
AHIMA Code of Ethics: safeguard the privacy, security, accessibility and integrity of health information.
Benefits: current EBP at hand, better quality and safety, help with health maintenance, coordinated care and information sharing, no paper referrals.
Technologic iatrogenesis: privacy breaches, poorly designed systems, research ethics, cyberattacks, accessibility problems, dilemmas from data sharing.
Autonomy: the patient controls who sees their information.
Nonmaleficence: avoid inaccurate charting and inappropriate sharing.
Justice: efficient EHRs and equitable access.
Copy-and-paste (content importing) from other providers, other patients or prior visits causes inaccuracy and legal liability.
Decision-support tools (diagnosis aids, drug recommendations, calculators) don't replace critical thinking.
Unanswered liability questions: a faulty EHR recommendation; a vendor's responsibility; a misleading display; ignoring alerts without documenting your reasoning.
No chart notes stored on devices that leave the facility
Teach patients about online information and unreliable sites, and caution them about buying prescriptions online.
Never post photos or PHI on social media, even if the patient isn't identifiable.
Don't complain online about patients or colleagues.
Don't require patients to sign a no-negative-review pledge. It is coercive.

Medicaid expansion varies by state; see the KFF tracker.
Regulatory agencies implement laws through rulemaking. They exist at the international, national, state and local level.
HHS agencies: CMS, OIG, OCR, ONC, FDA, CDC, NIOSH, SAMHSA, ASPR, HRSA, IHS.
Agency: CMS · Role: Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP; HIPAA compliance
Agency: AHRQ · Role: Research on quality, cost, patient safety and errors
Agency: CDC · Role: Public health surveillance and threats, vaccines, environmental and travel health
Agency: FDA · Role: Safety and effectiveness of drugs (human and animal), devices, biologics, food, cosmetics, supplements, the blood supply, recalls
Agency: NCQA (1991) · Role: Quality of managed care plans and HMOs
Agency: Joint Commission · Role: Accredits health care organizations
Agency: DEA · Role: Enforces controlled-substance law
Agency: NIOSH (part of CDC) · Role: Research on work-related disease and injury

Agency: OSHA · Role: Workplace safety standards and enforcement

Population health: outcomes and distribution of care for a group (by geography or special needs).
Community health: the health of people who live, work or play together.
Public health: collective work to protect communities through policy, education and outreach, and research.

Epidemiology studies how often disease occurs in groups and why. It describes the disease burden, finds causes and determinants, tests interventions, informs policy and evaluates programs. Its conclusions about a population at risk come from comparisons…
Epidemic: Limited in time and place · Pandemic: Spread over a larger area or many countries · Endemic: Constantly present over an extended period
Level: Primordial · Goal: Prevent risk factors from developing · Examples: Public health initiatives, school-based health, addressing SDOH, access to care
Level: Primary (PREVENT) · Goal: Prevent disease onset · Examples: Exercise, seatbelts, healthy-habit education, immunizations
Level: Secondary (SCREEN) · Goal: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment · Examples: Cancer screening, workplace modification, routine follow-up
Level: Tertiary (TREAT) · Goal: Minimize complications and disability · Examples: Chronic disease management, cardiac and vocational rehab
Healthy People 2030 (Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion) sets national goals over 10 years:
Long, high-quality lives free of preventable disease, disability, injury and early death.
Health equity and the elimination of disparities.
Social and physical environments that support health.
Healthy development and behaviors at every life stage.

Its principles are health equity, shared responsibility, data-driven objectives, and attention to social, physical and economic environments. It draws on EBP, epidemiology and the levels of prevention.

Nationally notifiable to CDC. Waterborne: cholera, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia, hepatitis A, Legionella, malaria, Salmonella, Shigella, typhoid, Vibrio, yellow fever. Others: cancer, chancroid, chlamydia, COVID-19, gonorrhea, HIV,…
State-reportable lists exist in every state. Reporting is the provider's responsibility.
Total case counts: e.g., chickenpox, influenza.
Cancer goes to the state cancer registry.
Mandatory reporters: health care providers, childcare workers, clergy, coaches and educators, counselors, law enforcement.
Covered populations: children (federal CAPTA), people with disabilities, older adults; intimate partners vary by state.
Scale: 1 in 8 children are affected, and homicide is a top-5 cause of child death. Intimate partner violence affects about 1 in 3 women and 17% of men. About 10% of adults ≥60 experience abuse.
Mandatory reporters must report suspicion. The burden of proof is NOT on the reporter.

ANA Standard 8: culturally congruent practice. "Health care isn't one-size-fits-all." Use shared decision-making that respects cultural norms, even when they may conflict with EBP, and identify the patient's cultural and language needs.

Culture is learned, shared knowledge that groups use to guide behavior and interpret the world: beliefs, interaction norms, morals, customs, technologies and survival strategies. It shapes work, parenting, marriage, and understanding of health, illness,…
Four components of culturally congruent care
Cultural diversity: age, gender, sexual orientation, SES, education, race, ethnicity, language, religion; differences between and within groups.
Cultural awareness (cognitive): understand what culture is, intracultural variation, and your own biases; reflect on your reactions.
Cultural responsiveness (affective): openness; no right or wrong values on differences.
Cultural competence (behavioral): a dynamic process of gaining knowledge and skills and adapting care.
Assimilation: one culture fully absorbs the other.
Acculturation: a group adopts some practices of the host culture but keeps identifiable differences.
Anticipatory guidance is education and proactive counseling that complements risk assessment: risk reduction, health promotion, disease prevention, complications. Use it for:
Advance care planning: goals, values and preferences; timelines; living will and durable power of attorney; organ donation; POLST/MOLST.
After-death wishes: will or trust, finances, funeral plans.
Palliative care: begins at diagnosis of a serious illness; disease treatment continues; the PCP stays involved; addresses symptoms and emotional, social, practical and spiritual needs.
Treatment discontinuation: when burdens outweigh benefits and goals shift from cure to comfort.
Hospice: comfort at the end of life, at home, in hospital or in a nursing home, after curative treatment stops; teaches caregivers what to expect.
Levels of influence on health behavior (education works best when it targets several levels)
Public policy: local, state and federal laws.

Health Belief Model. The manual shows it as an image; the constructs are standard. People act when they perceive susceptibility and severity, see benefits that outweigh barriers, encounter cues to action, and have self-efficacy.
Stage: Precontemplation · Definition: No intention to change · Strategy: Educate; personalize the risks and benefits
Stage: Contemplation · Definition: Aware of the problem and intends to act, but not committed · Strategy: Motivate; encourage specific plans
Stage: Preparation · Definition: Intends to act soon; has taken first steps · Strategy: Help build concrete action plans and goals
Stage: Action · Definition: Actively changing (<6 months) · Strategy: Feedback, reinforcement, problem-solving, social support
Stage: Maintenance · Definition: Change sustained (>6 months) · Strategy: Coping, reminders, alternatives, relapse prevention
Stage: Relapse · Definition: Falls back into old patterns · Strategy: Re-engage; the process is circular
Theory of planned behavior: behavioral intention is driven by attitude (is the behavior good or bad?), subjective norm (do key people approve?) and perceived behavioral control (is it up to me?).
Motivational interviewing (MI) is a guiding style between following and directing. It draws out the patient's own reasons for change, collaborates, and honors autonomy.
Partnership: the patient is the expert on their life.
Acceptance: nonjudgmental, empathetic, respects informed choices.
Evocation: people already have the resources to change.
Reflective listening: shows empathy and respect, not necessarily agreement
Evoking: draw out the patient's own "why."
Planning: an acceptable, accessible change plan.
Exosystem: indirect settings, such as a parent's workplace
Family systems theory (Murray Bowen) sees the family as an interconnected emotional unit with reciprocal relationships. Its 8 concepts:
Nuclear family emotional system (marital conflict, dysfunction in one spouse, impairment of a child, emotional distance)
Genogram: at least three generations, with ages, sex, medical, genetic, behavioral and social information. Look for red flags such as suicide, alcohol use and depression.
Ecomap: a picture of the family's ties to outside systems (school, work, worship, health care, recreation) and the strength of those ties.
Pedigree: symbols for affected or unaffected, alive or deceased.
Types: emotional, physical or sexual abuse; violence against a parent; household substance use; household mental illness or suicidality; an incarcerated household member.
Stress: positive, tolerable or toxic. ACEs rarely occur alone; 1 in 8 children have ≥4.
ACE pyramid: ACEs disrupt neurodevelopment, leading to social, emotional and cognitive impairment, health-risk behaviors, disease and disability, and early death.
Biologic: wear and tear; immunity; programmed longevity.
Sociologic: roles and relationships; disengagement; continuity; age stratification (cohorts such as baby boomers).
Psychologic: Erikson's integrity vs. despair; Maslow; Jung's individualism.
Moral or spiritual: how a person explains and validates their existence.
Access to care is "the timely use of personal health services to achieve the best health outcomes" (IOM, 1993). Healthy People 2030 names four components:

Component: Coverage · Meaning: Entry into the system; the uninsured get less care and are sicker · Barriers: Unaffordable or no employer coverage; high-deductible plans; few Medicaid providers; costs of drugs and tests; prior authorizations

Component: Services · Meaning: A usual source of care brings recommended screening · Barriers: Restrictive APRN practice laws; provider shortages; lack of culturally competent care; no broadband; signature authority; telehealth rules

Component: Timeliness · Meaning: Care when the need is recognized · Barriers: SDOH (income, geography, language, literacy); no choice of provider; transportation; signature authority delays; home health and telehealth barriers

Component: Workforce · Meaning: Capable, qualified, culturally competent providers · Barriers: Health Professional Shortage Areas (primary, mental, specialty care); Medically Underserved Areas; safety-net strain

resources for daily needs: education, jobs and living wages, healthy food
